provenance.rightsStatus: Primarily reference-only sources plus one public-domain federal court opinion and three CC BY articles; no source prose adapted, and all wording is original.
provenance.transformation: Written from independently verified facts drawn from the primary 1961 experimental report, an ERIC-indexed review of the Bobo doll programme, a scholarly overview of social cognitive theory, two federal IES practice guides, an ERIC-indexed review of peer modeling in education, three peer-reviewed open-access articles, an APA policy resolution, and a U.S. Supreme Court opinion. No source was paraphrase-followed; the generated draft was discarded entirely.

title: Motivation and Learning
in30Seconds: Motivation is not one dial that turns students up or down. Research treats it as several separable judgments: whether you expect to succeed, whether the task is worth what it costs, whose reason you are acting on, what you think caused your last result, and what you are counting as success. Self-determination theory, situated expectancy-value theory, attribution theory, and achievement goal theory each formalize one of those judgments, and each points at a different classroom move.
whyItMatters: Every teaching decision - how much choice to offer, how to word feedback, whether to grade on a curve, whether to pay students for reading - is a bet about what drives effort. Motivation research turns those bets into testable claims, and not all of the claims survive testing. Two of the field's most repeated ideas, that rewards poison interest and that a short mindset lesson lifts achievement, are contested in ways popular summaries rarely report. Reading the actual effect sizes, including the null results, is what separates a teacher who designs incentives deliberately from one who inherits a classroom ritual and never asks what it is doing. The vocabulary here also underwrites later work on assessment, engagement, and self-regulated learning.
learningObjectives: Define motivation in achievement settings in terms of direction, intensity, and persistence rather than as a single quantity.
Explain why the intrinsic/extrinsic binary is too crude, using self-determination theory's continuum of regulation and its three basic psychological needs.
Apply situated expectancy-value theory and attribution theory to diagnose why a specific student has disengaged.
Distinguish mastery from performance goals, including approach and avoidance forms, and explain why measurement choices complicate the comparison.
Evaluate what the evidence actually shows about extrinsic rewards and about growth mindset interventions, using reported effect sizes rather than slogans.

collegeVersion.heading: Motivation is a set of judgments, not a quantity
collegeVersion.body:
Calling a student unmotivated rarely survives contact with the student. The ninth grader who will not start a lab report may spend four hours on a drum part or a fantasy league roster, so the useful question is not how much motivation exists but where it points and why. Achievement motivation research therefore separates three things a theory has to predict: direction, meaning which task gets chosen; intensity, meaning how much effort goes in; and persistence, meaning what happens after the first bad result. A theory earns its place by predicting all three from something you can observe or change.

Four families of theory dominate the field, and they are complements rather than rivals. Self-determination theory asks why the student is doing the task. Expectancy-value theory asks whether the student expects to succeed and what the task is worth against what it costs. Attribution theory asks what the student believes caused the last outcome. Achievement goal theory asks what the student is treating as success in the first place. Self-efficacy - a person's judgment of their own capability on a specific task - runs underneath all four; it is developed in the social learning theory lesson, and here it matters mainly as the engine behind expectancy for success.

collegeVersion.heading: Why intrinsic versus extrinsic is too crude
collegeVersion.body:
Intrinsic motivation means doing something because the activity itself is interesting or satisfying. Extrinsic motivation means doing it for some outcome separable from the activity. Ryan and Deci's objection to stopping there is that extrinsic reasons differ enormously in how much they feel like the student's own, so a single label hides the variable that actually predicts behavior.

Self-determination theory arranges extrinsic reasons on a continuum of internalization. External regulation is compliance to get a reward or dodge a penalty; the reason lives outside the student. Introjected regulation is a rule swallowed but not digested: the student works to avoid guilt or shame or to protect self-worth, so the pressure is now internal without being freely chosen. Identified regulation is endorsement; the student may still find the task dull but genuinely values what it leads to. Integrated regulation is identification that sits consistently with the person's other values and sense of self.

The continuum is not decoration. A meta-analysis of 344 samples covering 223,209 students found that these types behave differently. Intrinsic motivation related to success and well-being. Identified regulation was especially strongly related to persistence. Introjected regulation predicted persistence and performance goals but also indicators of ill-being. External regulation was not associated with performance or persistence at all, and was associated with reduced well-being. One word, extrinsic, collapses at least three distinct patterns.

collegeVersion.heading: The three basic needs
collegeVersion.body:
Self-determination theory explains the continuum with three basic psychological needs. Autonomy is experiencing your own action as self-endorsed rather than coerced. It is not permissiveness, and it is not a menu: a requirement whose rationale a student accepts can support autonomy, while a choice among three trivial options usually does not. Competence is the sense that you can meet the demand, supported by work pitched near the edge of current ability and by feedback that says what to change. Relatedness is being connected to and mattering to the people in the room.

Meeting those needs is how a reason moves along the continuum from external toward identified. The standard classroom translation, as the open educational psychology literature states it, is to offer genuine choices, calibrate difficulty, give timely feedback, and build cooperative work. The competence-support half of this has federal backing of a modest kind: the 2007 IES practice guide on encouraging girls in math and science recommends prescriptive, informational feedback - telling a student specifically what to do differently rather than only how they did - and rates that recommendation as supported by moderate evidence.

collegeVersion.heading: Expectancy, value, and cost
collegeVersion.body:
Eccles, Wigfield, and colleagues have spent forty years on two questions: can I do this, and do I want to? Expectancy for success is a student's belief about how well they will do on an upcoming task; ability beliefs are the related judgment about current competence. Subjective task value breaks into attainment value, whether doing this well matters to who the student is; intrinsic value, whether they enjoy it; utility value, whether it gets them something they want; and cost. Cost has done increasing work in recent versions of the theory: time surrendered, effort required, anxiety incurred, and the other things not done instead. A student can rate a course as genuinely valuable and still walk away because the cost column is heavy.

In 2020 Eccles and Wigfield renamed the framework situated expectancy-value theory. The rename added no new machinery. Its point was to stop readers treating the familiar box-and-arrow diagram as static, linear, and monolithic, and to foreground how expectancies and values develop inside a particular situation and cultural background, shaped by the messages students receive from teachers, families, and peers, and by how students interpret their own past performance. Read that way, the claim that a student does not value mathematics turns into a question about what her setting has been telling her, and for how long.

collegeVersion.heading: Attributions: what the student thinks caused it
collegeVersion.body:
After a result arrives, students explain it. Weiner's attributional theory sorts those explanations by three dimensions rather than by content. Locus asks whether the cause is inside the person - ability, effort, strategy - or outside, such as task difficulty, luck, or a grader. Stability asks whether the cause will still be there next time. Controllability asks whether the person can influence it.

The dimensions predict what happens next better than the label does. I failed because I am not a math person is internal, stable, and uncontrollable, the combination that most reliably ends persistence, because nothing about the next attempt looks any different. I failed because I started the night before is internal, unstable, and controllable, which leaves a move on the board. Roughly, stability governs expectancy for the next attempt while controllability governs emotional responses and how others react.

Attribution retraining follows from this and is easy to do badly. Redirecting a student toward effort helps only when effort actually would have changed the outcome. If the real cause was a missing prerequisite or a poor strategy, try harder is both false and demoralizing, which is why the open literature pairs attribution work with appropriately difficult tasks, individual help, and the message that ability itself grows incrementally.

collegeVersion.heading: Goal orientation, and a measurement problem
collegeVersion.body:
Achievement goal theory asks what a student is treating as success. Mastery goals define it as understanding the material or improving on your own past performance. Performance goals define it relative to other people. Elliot and McGregor crossed that distinction with approach and avoidance to give four types: mastery-approach, pursuing understanding; mastery-avoidance, trying not to fail to learn or not to lose a skill; performance-approach, trying to outdo others; and performance-avoidance, trying not to look incompetent. Performance-avoidance is the one nearly everyone agrees is bad news, and it breeds self-handicapping, where a student procrastinates or visibly does not try so that a poor result implicates effort rather than ability.

The textbook summary is that mastery goals produce deeper, more durable learning while performance goals may still buy grades. Treat that as a first approximation, because the measures disagree with each other. A 2010 meta-analysis of 243 correlational studies with 91,087 participants found that goal-outcome correlations depended on which scale was used and how its items were worded: performance-approach scales built mostly from normatively referenced items correlated positively with performance outcomes, r = .14, while scales built mostly from appearance and evaluative items correlated negatively, r = -.14. The authors concluded that researchers are putting one label on conceptually different constructs. When you read that performance goals help or hurt, the first question is what the items actually said.

collegeVersion.heading: Two contested claims, reported honestly
collegeVersion.body:
Rewards. Pooling 128 experiments in 1999, Deci, Koestner, and Ryan reported that when students expected a tangible reward, their later free-choice engagement with the task fell - most sharply where the reward hung on merely taking part, d = -0.40 - while positive feedback pushed that same free-choice engagement up, d = 0.33. Critics replied that these detrimental effects appear only under restricted and easily avoidable conditions. The most usable synthesis is a 2014 meta-analysis of 183 samples and 212,468 participants: intrinsic motivation forecast performance both with incentives present and without them; that forecast weakened where the incentive hung directly on performance and held where it hung on performance only indirectly; and incentives tracked how much work got done while intrinsic motivation tracked how good it was. In the vocabulary of this lesson, a directly contingent payment installs external regulation in the place where you wanted identified regulation. The behaviorism lesson works through the same evidence from the contingency-design side.

Mindset. Dweck's implicit theories research holds that students who believe ability is malleable handle difficulty better than students who believe it is fixed, and short interventions have been claimed to raise achievement. The strongest test is the National Study of Learning Mindsets, a preregistered randomized trial with 12,490 ninth graders across 65 nationally representative U.S. schools. A single online session under an hour raised lower-achieving students' core-course GPA by 0.10 grade points and lifted enrollment in advanced tenth-grade mathematics from 33 percent to 36 percent, with effects concentrated in schools whose peer norms supported the message. That is real, targeted, and small. Meta-analyses find less. Sisk and colleagues, across a correlational analysis of 273 effects from 365,915 people and an intervention analysis of 43 effects from 57,155, reported weak overall effects with some support for benefits among low-socioeconomic-status or academically at-risk students. Macnamara and Burgoyne's 2023 review of 63 studies covering 97,672 students found an overall effect of d = 0.05 that was not significant after correcting for publication bias, d = 0.02 among the six highest-quality studies, and larger published effects from authors with a financial incentive to report them. The 2007 IES guide's recommendation to teach that academic abilities are expandable and improvable was rated moderate at the time; that rating predates every trial just described, which is a good reason to check the date on any recommendation.

vocabulary.definition: The processes that determine which activities a person chooses, how much effort they invest, and how long they keep going after difficulty.
The process by which a reason for acting that started outside the person becomes something they endorse and treat as their own.
Acting under internal pressure such as guilt, shame, or the need to protect self-worth, rather than from a freely chosen reason.
Acting because you personally value what the activity leads to, even if the activity itself holds no interest.
In self-determination theory, the three conditions - autonomy, competence, and relatedness - whose satisfaction supports interest and the internalization of external reasons.
A learner's belief about how well they will perform on an upcoming task, distinct from how much they want to do it.
How worthwhile an activity seems to a learner, made up of importance to identity, enjoyment, usefulness for other goals, and the costs incurred.
In situated expectancy-value theory, what pursuing a task takes away: time, effort, emotional strain, and the opportunities given up.
The explanation a person gives for why an outcome happened, classified by whether the cause is internal, lasting, and under their control.
What a learner is treating as success in a setting - improving on their own past, or comparing favorably with other people - and whether they are pursuing or avoiding it.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Instead of asking whether someone is motivated, ask four smaller questions. Do I think I can do this? People rarely start things they expect to fail at. Is it worth what it costs? Worth can mean fun, or useful, or important to who I am, and cost is the time, effort, and stress it takes. Whose reason is it? Doing homework because you would feel guilty otherwise is a different engine from doing it because you actually want what it leads to, even though neither one is fun. And what am I trying to prove? Trying to understand something and trying not to look stupid produce very different behavior once the work gets hard.
eli10.analogy: Deciding to cook a real dinner instead of ordering takeout works the same way. You need to believe the recipe is within your skill, you need to want the result enough - because it tastes good, because it saves money, or because you think of yourself as someone who cooks - and you weigh all that against the cost: the shopping, the hour, the sink full of pans. Change any one of those and the decision flips.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy makes motivation look like a conscious calculation made once, alone, with full information. It is usually none of those. A student's sense of what a subject is worth is built over years out of grades, offhand comments, and what their friends treat as normal, and it can shift inside one class period. A kitchen also has no audience deciding whether you belong in it, while relatedness - feeling connected to the people around you - is one of the three needs the research says has to be met.

workedExample: Hulleman and Harackiewicz ran a randomized field experiment in high school science classes. One randomly assigned group wrote short pieces connecting the unit's content to their own lives; the comparison group did not. The relevance writing raised interest in science and course grades, but the gain concentrated among students who had low expectations of success. Read that through situated expectancy-value theory. The intervention targeted utility value and left expectancy alone, so it paid off precisely for the students whose value was the binding constraint; students who already expected to do well had no shortage of value to add. That is the general lesson of diagnosis before intervention: find out whether the missing piece is expectancy, value, cost, or an unmet need, because the wrong repair does nothing at all.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sorting students into two boxes, intrinsically and extrinsically motivated.
commonMistakes.correction: Extrinsic reasons run along a continuum of internalization. Identified regulation is extrinsic and still autonomous, and in a meta-analysis of 344 samples it was the type most strongly related to persistence, while external regulation was unrelated to performance or persistence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating unmotivated as a stable description of a person.
commonMistakes.correction: Ask which judgment failed: does the student expect to fail, find the task worthless, find the cost too high, or lack autonomy, competence, or relatedness in that room? Each diagnosis implies a different move, and the label implies none.

commonMistakes.mistake: Telling every struggling student to try harder because effort attributions are the good kind.
commonMistakes.correction: Effort attributions help only when effort would actually have changed the result. If the barrier was a missing prerequisite or a bad strategy, the accurate and more useful response is prescriptive, informational feedback about what to do differently.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking mastery goals good, performance goals bad as a settled empirical result.
commonMistakes.correction: It is a reasonable first approximation, but a 2010 meta-analysis found performance-approach scales correlated with performance at r = .14 or r = -.14 depending only on how the items were worded. Ask what the measure said before generalizing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Presenting growth mindset interventions as a reliable way to raise achievement.
commonMistakes.correction: The best-powered national trial found a 0.10 grade-point gain limited to lower-achieving students in schools with supportive peer norms, and meta-analyses report weak to non-significant average effects with evidence of publication bias. Report it as contested.

compareContrast.distinction: Intrinsic motivation comes from the activity being interesting in itself; identified regulation comes from valuing what the activity leads to. Both are autonomous, which is why lumping identified regulation in with rewards and punishments as extrinsic loses the distinction that predicts persistence.

Expectancy is a prediction about performance; value is a judgment about worth. Neither one substitutes for the other: a student confident of an easy A can still skip a course they consider pointless, and a student who loves a subject can avoid it if they expect to fail.

Both define success by comparison with others, but approach goals aim at outperforming while avoidance goals aim only at not looking incompetent. Avoidance goals are the ones consistently tied to poor outcomes and to self-handicapping such as deliberate under-effort.

compareContrast.b: Attributing failure to a weak strategy
compareContrast.distinction: Both are internal, but ability is usually construed as stable and uncontrollable while strategy is unstable and controllable. The second leaves expectancy for the next attempt intact and names a specific thing to change; the first does neither.

keyTakeaway: Motivation is not one quantity to raise but a set of separable judgments - expectancy, value, cost, whose reason is driving the effort, and what counts as success - and the honest picture of the research includes contested findings, small effect sizes, and measures that disagree with one another.

questionBank.prompt: In self-determination theory's continuum of extrinsic motivation, which form best describes a student who completes assignments mainly to avoid feeling guilty or ashamed?
options: External regulation
Identified regulation
Introjected regulation
Integrated regulation
questionBank.explanation: Introjected regulation is the partially internalized form in which the pressure has moved inside the person - guilt, shame, or protecting self-worth - without being freely chosen. External regulation would mean working for a reward or to avoid a penalty imposed from outside; identified regulation would mean valuing what the work leads to; integrated regulation would mean that valuing sits consistently with the student's other values and sense of self.
questionBank.skill: Naming the forms of regulation on the internalization continuum

questionBank.prompt: Why did Eccles and Wigfield rename their framework situated expectancy-value theory in 2020?
options: They replaced expectancy and value with a single combined motivation score.
They wanted to stress that expectancies and values develop within particular situations and cultural contexts rather than being static, linear, and universal.
Later research showed that subjective task value does not predict which activities students choose.
They restricted the theory to laboratory studies of short-term task choice.
questionBank.explanation: The 2020 article argues that the standard diagram makes the model look static, linear, and monolithic, and uses the rename to foreground the situative and cultural formation of expectancies and values along with the elaborated cost component. The constructs were not merged or discarded, task value remains a central predictor of choice, and the framework is developmental and field-based rather than restricted to the laboratory.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting the current framing of expectancy-value theory

questionBank.prompt: A student says, "I bombed the chemistry test because I'm just not a science person." Using Weiner's dimensions, which reading of that attribution is accurate?
options: External, stable, and controllable, so the student is likely to blame the teacher and change strategy.
Internal, unstable, and controllable, so the student has left an obvious move available for next time.
External, unstable, and uncontrollable, so expectancy for the next test should be unaffected.
Internal, stable, and uncontrollable, the combination that most undermines expectancy for the next attempt.
questionBank.explanation: Not being a science person locates the cause in the person, treats it as permanent, and treats it as beyond influence. Because stability drives expectancy for the next attempt, that combination leaves the student with no reason to expect a different result and no specific thing to change. The other options misclassify at least one dimension: the cause is neither external nor unstable as the student has framed it.
questionBank.skill: Classifying a real attribution and predicting its motivational consequence

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best represents the current state of the evidence on growth mindset interventions?
options: Large randomized trials show that short mindset interventions produce large achievement gains for most students.

A nationally representative randomized trial found small, targeted gains for lower-achieving students in schools with supportive norms, while meta-analyses report weak or non-significant average effects.
Meta-analyses show that mindset interventions reduce achievement, so schools should abandon them.
No large-scale randomized evidence about mindset interventions has been collected.
questionBank.explanation: The National Study of Learning Mindsets found a 0.10 grade-point gain in core-course GPA for lower-achieving students and a three-percentage-point rise in advanced mathematics enrollment, concentrated where peer norms supported the message; Sisk and colleagues reported weak overall effects, and Macnamara and Burgoyne found d = 0.05 overall, non-significant after correcting for publication bias. So the effects are neither large, nor negative, nor absent from the record - they are small and conditional.
questionBank.skill: Weighing a large trial against meta-analytic evidence on a contested claim

questionBank.prompt: A science department wants better lab reports, not more of them, and proposes paying students a fixed amount for each report submitted. What does the meta-analytic evidence most support about this design?
options: Incentives tend to predict the quantity of work while intrinsic motivation better predicts its quality, so paying per report targets the wrong outcome and risks displacing the more autonomous reasons for writing well.
Because the payment is tangible and expected, the students' interest in science will be permanently destroyed.
Rewards have no measurable relationship to intrinsic motivation, so the design is motivationally neutral.
Praise and cash payment have the same measured effect on free-choice engagement, so the choice between them does not matter.
questionBank.explanation: The 2014 meta-analysis of 183 samples found that incentives better predict quantity of performance while intrinsic motivation better predicts quality, and that intrinsic motivation's contribution shrinks when incentives are tied directly to performance. The remaining options overstate the 1999 undermining result as permanent destruction, deny a large measured literature, or ignore that the 1999 meta-analysis found positive feedback raised free-choice engagement while expected tangible rewards lowered it.
questionBank.skill: Using contested reward evidence to evaluate an incentive design

provenance.rightsStatus: Reference-only scholarly sources plus one CC BY 3.0 open textbook and one U.S. federal practice guide; no source prose adapted, all wording original.
provenance.transformation: Abstracts and metadata verified through the Europe PMC, Crossref, and Semantic Scholar APIs, the open PMC full text of the Nature trial, the LibreTexts edition of a CC BY educational psychology chapter, and the IES practice-guide page cross-checked against the ERIC full text. Findings were synthesized into an original lesson; the reward-debate section reuses the same primary sources as the behaviorism lesson but frames them through the internalization continuum rather than contingency design.

quickCheck.prompt: In self-determination theory's continuum of extrinsic motivation, which form best describes a student who completes assignments mainly to avoid feeling guilty or ashamed?
options: External regulation
Identified regulation
Introjected regulation
Integrated regulation
quickCheck.explanation: Introjected regulation is the partially internalized form in which the pressure has moved inside the person - guilt, shame, or protecting self-worth - without being freely chosen. External regulation would mean working for a reward or to avoid a penalty imposed from outside; identified regulation would mean valuing what the work leads to; integrated regulation would mean that valuing sits consistently with the student's other values and sense of self.
quickCheck.skill: Naming the forms of regulation on the internalization continuum

quickCheck.prompt: Why did Eccles and Wigfield rename their framework situated expectancy-value theory in 2020?
options: They replaced expectancy and value with a single combined motivation score.
They wanted to stress that expectancies and values develop within particular situations and cultural contexts rather than being static, linear, and universal.
Later research showed that subjective task value does not predict which activities students choose.
They restricted the theory to laboratory studies of short-term task choice.
quickCheck.explanation: The 2020 article argues that the standard diagram makes the model look static, linear, and monolithic, and uses the rename to foreground the situative and cultural formation of expectancies and values along with the elaborated cost component. The constructs were not merged or discarded, task value remains a central predictor of choice, and the framework is developmental and field-based rather than restricted to the laboratory.
quickCheck.skill: Interpreting the current framing of expectancy-value theory

quickCheck.prompt: A student says, "I bombed the chemistry test because I'm just not a science person." Using Weiner's dimensions, which reading of that attribution is accurate?
options: External, stable, and controllable, so the student is likely to blame the teacher and change strategy.
Internal, unstable, and controllable, so the student has left an obvious move available for next time.
External, unstable, and uncontrollable, so expectancy for the next test should be unaffected.
Internal, stable, and uncontrollable, the combination that most undermines expectancy for the next attempt.
quickCheck.explanation: Not being a science person locates the cause in the person, treats it as permanent, and treats it as beyond influence. Because stability drives expectancy for the next attempt, that combination leaves the student with no reason to expect a different result and no specific thing to change. The other options misclassify at least one dimension: the cause is neither external nor unstable as the student has framed it.
quickCheck.skill: Classifying a real attribution and predicting its motivational consequence

title: Memory and Learning
in30Seconds: Memory is not one store, and forgetting is not one process. Encoding, storage, and retrieval fail in different ways and need different repairs. Long-term memory splits into memory for events, memory for facts, and memory for skills. Most study time goes into rereading and highlighting, which the evidence rates poorly, while the two techniques that survive every test - spacing practice out and retrieving instead of reviewing - feel harder and get used least.
whyItMatters: Teacher preparation hands you two accounts of memory that look alike and are not: a folk psychology built from metaphors of recording and storage, and a research literature that has spent a century measuring what actually survives. The gap between them is where bad study advice lives. Students who reread until a page feels familiar are measuring fluency, not learning, and they keep doing it because it works on Friday's quiz and fails on June's final. Knowing how retrieval, spacing, and interference behave lets you build a review schedule instead of improvising one, explain to a student why a method failed, and recognise the memory myths that still circulate in staff rooms and professional development slides.
learningObjectives: Distinguish encoding, storage, and retrieval failures, and use cue-supported recall to tell an inaccessible memory from an absent one.
Describe the components of Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model and the declarative/nondeclarative division of long-term memory, and explain what each division predicts about assessment.
Explain the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve together with the methodological limits of the single-subject nonsense-syllable studies that produced it, including the 2015 replication.
Analyse a case of forgetting in terms of decay, interference, and retrieval failure, and identify which explanation the available evidence supports.
Apply the Dunlosky et al. (2013) utility ratings to evaluate or redesign a student's study plan, including where interleaving should not be used.
Evaluate the claims that we use ten percent of our brain and that memory records experience, and state precisely what reconstructive memory does and does not imply.

collegeVersion.heading: Three stages, three different failures
collegeVersion.body: Memory research separates the initial learning of information, its persistence over time, and the act of getting it back. The separation earns its keep because all three failures look identical from outside - a student who cannot answer - while each calls for a different response. Material never attended to was never encoded. Material encoded but never consolidated may genuinely be gone. Material still present but unreachable is a retrieval problem, and retrieval problems are the ones a teacher can usually solve, because retrieval runs on cues. The National Academies' How People Learn II puts the point in a form worth keeping: retrieval is triggered and guided by the retrieval cues available in the learner's environment, so what a student can produce depends on what the question and the format offer her. That gives you a ten-second diagnostic. Offer a hint. If the answer arrives, the memory was there all along and only unreachable - the trace existed, the route did not. Psychologists mark this as the difference between what is available in storage and what is accessible right now, and it runs underneath everything else in this lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Working memory has parts, and long-term memory has kinds
collegeVersion.body: How much fits in working memory at once, and how to design materials around that limit, is the subject of the cognitivism lesson in this subject; this section is about structure rather than size. Baddeley and Hitch's multicomponent model divides temporary storage by code instead of treating it as one box. A phonological loop holds verbal and acoustic material - the inner voice repeating a phone number. A visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial material. A central executive directs attention among them and controls what gets manipulated. In 2000 Baddeley added a fourth component, the episodic buffer, a limited store that binds material from the subsystems and from long-term memory into integrated episodes. The framework replaced a single short-term store because working memory does not merely hold information, it operates on it. Long-term memory is likewise not one thing. Squire and Dede split it into declarative memory, knowledge available to conscious recollection and dependent on the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe, and nondeclarative memory, an umbrella covering skills and habits in the striatum, priming, emotional associations in the amygdala, and classical conditioning in the cerebellum. Declarative memory subdivides again into episodic memory for specific events located in time and place, and semantic memory for facts detached from the occasion of learning them. The clinching evidence is patient H.M., who after medial temporal lobe surgery could not form new declarative memories yet still acquired motor skills across days of practice, improving at a task he had no recollection of ever performing. Memory, in Squire's phrase, is not a single entity. The classroom consequence follows directly: a student can execute a titration flawlessly and be unable to say what it demonstrates, and if your objective names a skill, a definitional test will not measure it.

collegeVersion.heading: Depth of processing, and the problem it never solved
collegeVersion.body: Craik and Lockhart's 1972 levels-of-processing framework proposed that retention is a byproduct of how material is analysed rather than of how long it is held. Analysing surface form - what a word looks like, what it rhymes with - leaves a weaker trace than analysing meaning. The practical instruction that follows is the framework's most durable contribution and is still what the open memory literature tells students: at study, think about the meaning of the material, form associations, and build vivid mental images. Elaborate, do not repeat. The theoretical core is shakier, and Craik said so himself. His 2002 retrospective takes up the standing criticisms directly: whether memory can be treated as pure processing, how depth could be measured, how encoding and retrieval conditions interact, and whether levels are real in any strong sense. The sharpest objection is circularity - if depth is inferred from how well material was remembered, and remembering is then explained by depth, the framework has redescribed the result rather than explained it. Treat levels of processing as a reliable heuristic for designing study tasks, not a dial with units on it.

collegeVersion.heading: The forgetting curve, told honestly
collegeVersion.body: In 1879 and 1880 Hermann Ebbinghaus ran 163 double tests on himself, learning eight series of thirteen nonsense syllables (six in some sessions) until he could recite them twice without error and then relearning them after about a third of an hour, an hour, nine hours, one day, two days, six days, or thirty-one days. He measured retention as savings: the proportion of the original learning work he no longer needed on relearning. The result is the curve everyone has seen - a steep early drop flattening into a long tail. Roughly 58 percent of the work was saved after twenty minutes, 44 percent after an hour, 34 percent after a day, a quarter after six days, and about a fifth after a month. Now the caveats, the first of which is Ebbinghaus's own: he called the numbers special, individual, and uncertain, and judged the 33.7 percent one-day value one or two points too high. Second, the sample was one person, himself. Third, the material was deliberately meaningless - he chose nonsense syllables because ordinary words and poetry evoked variable meanings and added measurement error, which is to say he engineered out the feature that most defines classroom material. Murre and Dros tested the curve again in 2015 with the same method: one subject, about seventy hours of learning and relearning across the same seven intervals. Their curve closely resembled Ebbinghaus's at nearly every point, diverging sharply only at thirty-one days, where savings fell to 0.041 against Ebbinghaus's 0.211, and they concluded the curve is not perfectly smooth, most likely jumping upward around the twenty-four-hour point. So the shape is real and has been reproduced across more than a century; the numbers describe one person relearning meaningless syllables. Cite the shape, not the percentages.

collegeVersion.heading: Why we forget: decay, interference, retrieval failure
collegeVersion.body: Three explanations compete, and a fourth possibility - that the material was never encoded - has to be ruled out first. Decay theory says traces fade with the passage of time. It is the oldest account and the weakest, because disuse does not reliably produce forgetting; contemporary versions talk about consolidation being disrupted rather than about time doing the damage. Interference says memories compete. Proactive interference is older learning blocking newer: the first two conjugation patterns make the third harder to acquire. Retroactive interference is newer blocking older: the third pattern makes the first two harder to retrieve. Retrieval failure says the memory is intact but the cue inadequate, which is what a tip-of-the-tongue state is. All three contribute, and the honest position is that they are not tidy rivals. What matters for teaching is that they are distinguishable in practice. Give a cue: if the answer comes back, you were looking at retrieval failure, and the fix is retrieval practice under varied cues rather than more exposure. Look at what was learned nearby: if the errors are systematic confusions between similar items rather than blanks, you are looking at interference, and the fix is to separate confusable material in time and practise the discrimination directly.

collegeVersion.heading: Encoding specificity, and what context really buys you
collegeVersion.body: The encoding specificity principle states that a cue is effective to the degree that it overlaps the memory trace of the original experience. It is the most usable idea in the retrieval literature, and it is routinely oversold. The famous demonstration is Godden and Baddeley's 1975 study of divers who learned word lists on land or underwater and recalled them in the same or the other environment; watch what happened to it. Smith and Vela's 2001 meta-analysis found environmental context effects reliable overall but heavily moderated - they shrink when learners use non-contextual cues during study (overshadowing), when such cues are available at test (outshining), and when learners simply imagine the original setting at test. Then in 2021 Jaap Murre reran the diving experiment with sixteen divers and failed to replicate it: the crucial interaction between learning and recall environment was not significant, F = 1.999, p = 0.163. A 2022 addendum reanalysed the data as a repeated-measures ANOVA with an order covariate, which did make the interaction significant at p = 0.017, but in a pattern that did not match the original, and Murre restated that the replication was unsuccessful. So separate two claims that get bundled together. The principle - cues work in proportion to their overlap with what was encoded - is well supported and directly actionable. The strong environmental version, that a student must be tested where she studied, is not something to build practice on. Match the cues that carry meaning: practise retrieving in the format, with the prompt wording, and against the kind of question the assessment will use.

collegeVersion.heading: What actually works, in order
collegeVersion.body: Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham reviewed ten study techniques in 2013, judging each against four dimensions: learning conditions, student characteristics, materials, and criterion tasks. Two earned high utility - practice testing and distributed practice - because their benefits held across ages, abilities, materials, and outcome measures, including in real educational settings. Three earned moderate utility: elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, and interleaved practice. Five earned low utility: summarisation, highlighting and underlining, the keyword mnemonic, imagery use for text learning, and rereading. Read the middle tier correctly - moderate means thin evidence, not demonstrated failure. The testing effect is the anchor result. Roediger and Karpicke had students read prose passages and then either take immediate free-recall tests with no feedback or restudy the passage the same number of times. Five minutes later, restudying won. At two days and one week, the tested students retained substantially more, while the restudying students were the more confident group. That reversal is the finding to carry around: immediate fluency and durable retention can point in opposite directions. Spacing is the other high-utility technique, and Cepeda's meta-analysis of 839 assessments across 317 experiments in 184 articles established the design rule - the gap between study sessions that maximises final retention grows as the delay before the test grows. Interleaving needs the most care, because a later meta-analysis sharpened it. Brunmair and Richter pooled 59 studies and 238 effect sizes across 158 samples and found a moderate overall benefit, Hedges' g = 0.42, with the material doing most of the work: 0.67 for paintings and other visual categories, 0.34 for mathematics, non-significant for expository texts, and minus 0.39 for word learning, where blocking beat interleaving. So interleave problem types and categories that students confuse; do not interleave a vocabulary list. Elaborative interrogation - asking why a stated fact is true - and self-explanation - saying how a new idea relates to what you know - work by forcing generation rather than recognition. The two techniques students report using most, rereading and highlighting, do not consistently improve performance, and the recommendation is substitution rather than addition: practice testing instead of rereading, not after it.

collegeVersion.heading: Two myths, and one precise correction
collegeVersion.body: The claim that we use ten percent of our brain is false, and teachers believe it. Dekker and colleagues surveyed 242 teachers interested enough in the neuroscience of learning to take part - 137 in the United Kingdom, 105 in the Netherlands - and 48 percent and 46 percent respectively endorsed it. The refutation is straightforward. The brain is about two percent of body weight and consumes roughly twenty percent of the body's calories, and that consumption does not drop when a task is simple or when a person is asleep. Recovery after the loss of an entire hemisphere in early childhood reflects rewiring, not spare capacity sitting idle. The idea appears to descend from William James's 1907 remark that people use only a small part of their possible resources - a claim about effort, not anatomy. The second myth is subtler, because the correction gets overstated in turn. How People Learn II rejects the file-cabinet picture outright: memory systems give people the ability to produce knowledge without storing copies of it, and memories are reconstructed anew each time they are recalled, taking into account current knowledge, expectations, and context. Loftus's thirty-year programme on the misinformation effect shows the consequence - memory for an event is impaired by misleading information encountered afterwards, warnings help only in limited circumstances, and people can be led to believe they experienced complex events that never happened. Be precise about what that licenses. Reconstruction does not mean memory is generally unreliable; the same systems support accurate recall constantly. It means retrieval is an active process that can incorporate material from outside the original episode, so confidence is not a reliable index of accuracy. The classroom corollary is uncomfortable and useful: a confidently recalled misconception feels exactly like a confidently recalled fact, which is an argument for retrieval practice with feedback rather than retrieval practice alone.

vocabulary.definition: The rule that a hint or prompt helps in proportion to how much it overlaps with what was actually registered at the time of learning.
Ebbinghaus's measure of retention: the proportion of the original learning effort no longer needed when the same material is learned a second time.
Conscious recollection of particular events from one's own life, located in a specific time and place.
Conscious knowledge of facts, concepts, and word meanings, held independently of when or where it was acquired.
A form of nondeclarative memory expressed in performance rather than recollection, covering motor and cognitive skills and habits.
Disruption in which material learned earlier competes with and blocks newer, related material.
Disruption in which recently learned material competes with and blocks the recall of older, related material.
The finding that attempting to recall studied material improves later retention more than restudying it for the same amount of time.
A practice schedule that mixes problems or categories together rather than completing all of one kind before moving to the next.
Craik and Lockhart's framework holding that retention depends on whether material was analysed for meaning or only for surface features.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Your brain does not save a copy of a lesson the way a phone saves a photo. It keeps a web of connections, and remembering means rebuilding the thing out of that web. That is why three completely different things can go wrong. Sometimes you never built it, because you were not really paying attention. Sometimes you built it and it came apart. And sometimes it is still in there but you cannot find the way to it, which is why one small hint can bring back a name you were sure you had lost for good. Studying works best when you practise the rebuilding instead of practising the looking.
eli10.analogy: Learning something is like wearing a path across a field of tall grass. Every time you walk it yourself, the path gets clearer and easier to find again. Rereading your notes is like standing at the edge of the field looking at a photo of the path. It feels familiar, and it does almost nothing to the grass. Testing yourself is walking it. Spacing your practice out is coming back before the grass has grown all the way in, so each trip does real work.
eli10.analogyLimits: The path picture gets two things wrong. Real memories are not fixed routes. Each time you walk one you can change it a little, so a memory can come back altered after you hear someone else's version of the story - a path cannot pick up a bend from a rumour. And a field has one kind of ground, while memory has several systems that behave differently. Remembering your first day of school, knowing that a triangle has three sides, and being able to ride a bike run on different machinery, and damage that wipes out one can leave the others working fine.

workedExample: A student has a cumulative biology final in six weeks and plans to reread the textbook chapters twice, highlighting as she goes. Rebuild the plan from the utility ratings. Rereading and highlighting are both low utility, so they get substituted rather than supplemented. Weeks one to five: after each chapter she closes the book and free-recalls everything she can onto blank paper, then checks against the text and corrects what she got wrong - practice testing with feedback, so retrieval strengthens the right answer rather than her guess. She revisits each chapter on a widening schedule instead of once, because Cepeda's synthesis shows the optimal gap grows with the retention interval, and her interval is six weeks. Cell respiration and photosynthesis, which she keeps confusing, get interleaved in mixed practice sets and compared directly, since interference concentrates on similar material. Vocabulary drilling stays blocked - Brunmair and Richter found interleaving hurt word learning. For each process she asks why each step must happen in that order, which is elaborative interrogation. Final week: full practice exams in the format the real test will use, matching cues to the assessment rather than to her notes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Quoting the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve as the rate at which students forget lessons - for instance, telling teachers that pupils lose about 70 percent of a lesson within a day.
commonMistakes.correction: The curve's shape has replicated, but its percentages come from single-subject studies in which one man relearned deliberately meaningless syllables using the savings method. Ebbinghaus himself called the values special, individual, and uncertain. Use the shape as a reason to schedule early review; do not quote the numbers as classroom forecasts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging a study method by how fluent it feels, so that rereading and highlighting keep their place because the material feels familiar afterwards.
commonMistakes.correction: Roediger and Karpicke found restudying beat testing after five minutes and lost badly after two days and a week, while the restudying students were the more confident group. Fluency in the moment and retention at the delay can point in opposite directions, so the felt sense of knowing is not evidence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Interleaving everything once you learn that interleaving works, including vocabulary and word lists.
commonMistakes.correction: Brunmair and Richter's meta-analysis found a moderate average benefit but a reversal for word materials, where blocking outperformed interleaving. Interleave problem types and categories learners confuse; keep straightforward word learning blocked.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading reconstructive memory as proof that memory is generally unreliable, or, in the other direction, treating a confident recollection as a recording of what happened.
commonMistakes.correction: Memory produces knowledge rather than replaying stored copies, and post-event information can alter what is recalled - so confidence is not an index of accuracy. That does not make everyday recall untrustworthy. The teaching consequence is narrower and more useful: retrieval practice needs feedback, because unchecked retrieval strengthens whatever the student produced, including the misconception.

commonMistakes.mistake: Repeating that we only use ten percent of our brain, or implying students have untapped memory capacity waiting to be unlocked.
commonMistakes.correction: Roughly half the teachers in Dekker's UK and Dutch samples endorsed this, and it is false. The brain is about two percent of body weight and uses about twenty percent of the body's calories, activity continues throughout the brain during sleep, and the idea traces to a remark by William James about unused effort, not unused tissue.

compareContrast.distinction: Both are declarative and consciously accessible, but episodic memory reinstates a particular event in time and place, while semantic memory holds facts stripped of the occasion on which they were learned. A student can lose the memory of the lesson and keep the content.

Declarative memory is expressed by saying or recognising; procedural memory is expressed by doing. They depend on different brain systems, which is why H.M. could improve at a motor skill across days while having no recollection of practising it.

Decay claims the trace is gone; retrieval failure claims the trace is intact but unreached. The test is a cue: if a hint restores the answer, nothing had decayed, and the fix is retrieval practice rather than reteaching.

Both involve competition between similar memories; the direction differs. Proactive means older material obstructs newer, retroactive means newer material obstructs older. Which one you have determines whether the fix is spacing the new material out or re-establishing the old.

Blocking finishes one kind of problem before starting the next; interleaving mixes them. Interleaving helps most when categories are confusable and the material is complex, and it can hurt for simple word learning, so the schedule should follow the material rather than a slogan.

compareContrast.b: The claim that students should be tested where they studied
compareContrast.distinction: The principle - cues help in proportion to their overlap with encoding - is well supported. The environmental version is fragile: meta-analytic context effects shrink under overshadowing, outshining, and mental reinstatement, and the famous diving study failed to replicate in 2021. Match the format and the prompts, not the furniture.

keyTakeaway: Treat memory as three separable processes running over several distinct systems, and study strategy follows from the diagnosis: retrieval failures need cued practice, interference needs separation and discrimination, and the methods that feel hardest - self-testing and spaced review - are the two the evidence rates highest.

questionBank.prompt: In Baddeley and Hitch's multicomponent working memory model, which component was added in 2000, and what does it do?
options: The central executive, which directs attention among the storage subsystems.
The phonological loop, which holds verbal and acoustic material.
The episodic buffer, a limited store that binds information from the subsystems and from long-term memory into integrated episodes.
The visuospatial sketchpad, which holds visual and spatial material.
questionBank.explanation: The original 1974 model had three components: the central executive, the phonological loop, and the visuospatial sketchpad. The episodic buffer was added in 2000 as a temporary store that integrates information across different sensory codes and links working memory to long-term memory. The other three options name real components of the model, but each predates the 2000 revision.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the structure of the multicomponent working memory model

questionBank.prompt: A professional development slide states that students forget about two thirds of a lesson within twenty-four hours, citing the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve. What is the strongest objection?
options: The curve has never been replicated, so no part of it should be used.

The percentages come from single-subject experiments in which nonsense syllables were relearned by the savings method, so the shape generalises but the specific rates do not describe meaningful classroom material.
Ebbinghaus measured recognition rather than recall, which always produces lower scores than free recall.
The curve describes forgetting only in adults over sixty, so it cannot be applied to school-age learners.
questionBank.explanation: Murre and Dros replicated the curve closely in 2015, so option A is wrong. Ebbinghaus measured savings on relearning, not recognition, ruling out C, and he tested only himself rather than a sample of older adults, ruling out D. The real problem is generalisation: one person relearning deliberately meaningless syllables, with Ebbinghaus himself calling the values special, individual, and uncertain and judging the one-day figure too high. The shape is reproducible; the rates are not classroom forecasts.
questionBank.skill: Judging how far a classic result generalises from its methodology

questionBank.prompt: A student preparing for a cumulative exam in six weeks currently rereads each chapter twice and highlights as she goes. Which revision is best supported by the utility ratings and the underlying studies?
options: Keep the rereading and add highlighting in a second colour to mark the most important passages.
Reread each chapter three times instead of twice, since repeated exposure is what produced retention in the testing-effect experiments.
Keep rereading as the main method but take one practice test the night before the exam to check readiness.
Replace rereading with closed-book recall of each chapter followed by checking and correcting against the text, and revisit chapters on a widening schedule across the six weeks.
questionBank.explanation: Rereading and highlighting are both low-utility techniques, and the explicit recommendation is substitution rather than addition, which rules out A and C. Option B inverts Roediger and Karpicke's result: repeated studying beat testing only on the five-minute test and lost at two days and one week. Option D combines the two high-utility techniques - practice testing with feedback and distributed practice - and matches Cepeda's finding that the optimal gap between sessions grows with the retention interval.
questionBank.skill: Redesigning a study plan from evidence on technique utility

questionBank.prompt: A language teacher has read that interleaving improves learning and proposes to interleave the weekly vocabulary list with grammar exercises and cultural readings. What does the meta-analytic evidence most support?
options: Interleaving benefits vary sharply by material: the average effect is moderate, but for word learning blocking outperformed interleaving, so the vocabulary list is the wrong target while confusable grammar patterns are a good one.
Interleaving produces a large benefit for all verbal material, so the proposal should be adopted in full.
Interleaving has no reliable effect in any domain, so the schedule makes no difference.
Interleaving works only for mathematics and should never be used outside quantitative subjects.
questionBank.explanation: Brunmair and Richter found a moderate overall effect, Hedges' g = 0.42, but strongly moderated by material: 0.67 for paintings and other visual categories, 0.34 for mathematics, non-significant for expository texts, and minus 0.39 for words, where blocking won. That rules out B, C, and D. The defensible application is to interleave confusable categories and problem types while leaving straightforward vocabulary learning blocked.
questionBank.skill: Applying moderator findings rather than an average effect to an instructional decision

questionBank.prompt: A student cannot name the enzyme involved in a reaction, but produces it immediately when the teacher says it begins with a soft sound. What does this show, and what follows for instruction?
options: The trace had decayed and was reconstructed from the hint, so the material must be retaught from the beginning.
The memory was available but not accessible, indicating retrieval failure rather than loss, so the fix is practice retrieving it under varied cues rather than more exposure.
It shows retroactive interference, because a later-learned enzyme name blocked the earlier one.
It shows that the student never encoded the material and was guessing from the phonetic hint alone.
questionBank.explanation: Recovery from a cue is the standard demonstration that a memory is available in storage but not accessible with the cues previously on offer - retrieval failure, not decay or encoding failure, which rules out A and D. Nothing in the scenario identifies a competing later-learned item, so C is unsupported. Because retrieval is cue-driven, the productive response is repeated retrieval practice under varied prompts rather than re-presenting the content.
questionBank.skill: Diagnosing a forgetting episode and selecting the matching remedy

Replace rereading with closed-book recall of each chapter followed by checking and correcting against the text, and revisit chapters on a widening schedule across the six weeks.

Option B inverts Roediger and Karpicke's result: repeated studying beat testing only on the five-minute test and lost at two days and one week. Option D combines the two high-utility techniques - practice testing with feedback and distributed practice - and matches Cepeda's finding that the optimal gap between sessions grows with the retention interval.
