title: History and Role of Policing
in30Seconds: Modern policing is younger than most people assume. London got a full-time uniformed force in 1829; northern American cities built municipal departments between the 1830s and the 1850s, while southern colonies had already created armed slave patrols a century earlier. What police do has been redefined repeatedly since, and research from the 1970s onward showed that random patrol, heavy investigative effort, and fast response each did less than the profession assumed.
whyItMatters: Nearly every argument about American policing rests on a historical claim: that police were created to fight crime, to manage disorder, or to control enslaved people. Some of those claims are documented, some are contested, and some are folklore. Knowing which is which lets you read the argument instead of choosing a side by instinct. The same holds for the job itself. Staffing, training, and reform proposals all assume a picture of how officers spend their shifts, and measured pictures have looked different from assumed ones since the 1970s. This lesson gives you the dates, the studies, and the places where careful historians genuinely disagree.
learningObjectives: Trace the English antecedents of modern policing and explain what the Metropolitan Police Act 1829 actually established.
Explain why the nine 'Peelian principles' carry Peel's name and why the UK government itself disputes that attribution.
Distinguish the northern municipal and southern slave-patrol lineages of American policing and describe how historians weigh them against each other.
Summarize the Kelling and Moore three-era periodization and the published criticism that it is too tidy.
Evaluate what the Kansas City, RAND, and response-time studies found, including the limits their own authors stated.
Analyze call-for-service and police-contact data to describe what the police workload is actually composed of.

collegeVersion.heading: Before there was a police force
collegeVersion.body:
English policing grew out of shared obligation rather than paid employment. Households were grouped into tithings of ten families, tithings into hundreds, and hundreds into shires supervised by a shire-reeve, ancestor of the American sheriff. The constable, appointed locally and responsible for the hundred's weapons, is the earliest figure the 1967 President's Commission on Law Enforcement identifies as a police officer. Under Edward I (1272-1307) larger towns acquired a 'watch and ward' that guarded gates and arrested night-time offenders, and in 1326 Edward II created the office of justice of the peace; the constable became the justice's subordinate, a hierarchy that held for roughly five centuries.

By the eighteenth century the arrangement had decayed. Service everyone owed became service nobody performed: constables paid substitutes to take their turns, and the Commission describes those substitutes as badly paid and often too old to be effective. Night watchmen nominally guarded cities against thieves but reportedly did little beyond calling out the hour. Industrialising London improvised: government created public offices, later called police offices, each with three paid justices authorised to employ six paid constables, and civic bodies formed patrols such as the Bow Street Horse and Foot Patrol. By 1800 nine such offices existed in metropolitan London, and the Commission records that they largely refused to communicate with one another for fear of losing credit for an arrest. That is what 1829 was meant to solve: not the absence of law enforcement, but the absence of a coordinated, full-time, publicly accountable one.

collegeVersion.heading: 1829, and the principles Peel probably did not write
collegeVersion.body:
Robert Peel became Home Secretary in 1822 arguing that better policing could not eliminate crime but that bad policing was feeding disorder. Seven years later he steered through Parliament an Act for improving the police in and near the metropolis, recorded by legislation.gov.uk as the Metropolitan Police Act 1829, 1829 c. 44 in the tenth year of George IV. The force numbered about a thousand uniformed men under two magistrates, later titled commissioners, who held administrative but deliberately not judicial power, answering to the Home Secretary and through him to Parliament. An 1839 statute let county justices establish forces; an 1856 statute required every borough and county to have one.

The famous nine 'Peelian principles' are a separate matter, and their provenance is genuinely disputed. The Home Office's own published note on policing by consent states that there is no evidence of any link to Robert Peel, that the principles were likely devised by the first Commissioners of Police of the Metropolis, Charles Rowan and Richard Mayne, and that they were set out in the General Instructions issued to every new officer from 1829. Keep the distinction clean: the ideas the list expresses - that the police are the public, that cooperation falls as force is used, that the test of policing is the absence of crime rather than visible action - are real and old. The claim that Peel wrote them is the part that does not survive checking.

collegeVersion.heading: Two American lineages, and the argument between them
collegeVersion.body:
Colonists imported constables and sheriffs largely unchanged. Boston had night watchmen by 1636; New York's carried rattles and were known as the Rattlewatch. As cities grew, the watch failed the way the English one had. Boston created a day force in 1838 alongside its watch. The New York legislature passed a law in 1844 authorising the first unified day-and-night police and abolishing the watch; the standard list dates the resulting department to 1845. Boston consolidated in 1854. Hubert Williams and Patrick Murphy, writing in the same NIJ series, reproduce the conventional sequence of 'new police' dates, which begins Boston 1838, New York City 1845 and Chicago 1851 and runs on to Detroit in 1865.

Their central point is that this list is not the whole country. Southern colonial legislatures had enacted slave patrol statutes decades earlier - South Carolina in the 1740s, Georgia in 1757 - creating compulsory patrols empowered to search the dwellings of enslaved people for weapons, punish anyone found off a plantation without a pass, and enter houses suspected of harbouring or trading with them. Charleston, Savannah and Richmond ran combined foot and mounted patrols, and in Charleston policing was the largest single item in the municipal budget. Williams and Murphy report, attributing the argument to the historians Samuel Walker and Philip Reichel, that a strong case exists that the first American modern-style policing occurred in the slave patrols.

Hold that claim's shape precisely, because it is easy to overstate in either direction. It is documented that specific southern jurisdictions built permanent, publicly authorised, continuously patrolling forces for racial control before northern cities built municipal departments, and that there the patrol is a real institutional ancestor. It is an interpretive argument, not a settled finding, that this makes slave patrols the origin of American policing as a whole; Boston's and New York's departments have their own traceable descent from the watch. Williams and Murphy also note that northern departments were created amid anti-abolitionist and anti-Catholic rioting in the 1830s and 1840s, so even the northern story is more about controlling disorder than detecting crime. Historians differ over how much weight each strand carries, and a lesson that resolves that disagreement for you is doing you a disservice.

collegeVersion.heading: Three eras, and the criticism of the periodization
collegeVersion.body:
The standard map of American police history is the one George Kelling and Mark Moore published for NIJ in November 1988. Their political era, from the introduction of police into municipalities in the 1840s to the early 1900s, drew authority from ward politicians, defined the function broadly enough to include soup lines and lodging for newly arrived immigrants, ran through semi-autonomous precincts on foot patrol, and measured success as political and citizen satisfaction. Its weaknesses were corruption, curbstone justice against outsiders, and almost no supervisory control.

The reform era took hold in the 1930s, peaked in the 1950s and 1960s, and eroded in the late 1970s. August Vollmer, chief in Berkeley, rallied executives around reform in the 1920s and 1930s, and his protege O.W. Wilson became its principal administrative architect. Reformers replaced political authorization with law and professionalism, used civil service to break patronage hiring, narrowed the function to crime control, and organised departments on Taylorist lines. Wilson supplied the theory that marked cars patrolling randomly would create a sense of police omnipresence, and departments pushed centralized dispatch and 911, marketing rapid response as effective crime control. The 1967 President's Commission ratified the shift by recasting police as part of a criminal justice system rather than an agency of city government. The third era, community problem solving, widens the function again toward order maintenance and problem solving.

Kelling and Moore themselves warn that the boundaries are not clean. The sharper criticism came from Williams and Murphy in 1990, in the same series, who called the analysis 'disturbingly incomplete': it takes little account of slavery, segregation and discrimination, treats departments as autonomous strategists rather than as barometers of the society around them, and generalises from the urban Northeast. Use the three eras as a filing system for changes in authorization, function, organisation and tactics, not as a chronology every department passed through on schedule.

collegeVersion.heading: The studies that dismantled the reform-era assumptions
collegeVersion.body:
Three studies did more than any argument to unsettle the professional model, and each is routinely misquoted, so specifics matter. The Kansas City Preventive Patrol Experiment ran from 1 October 1972 to 30 September 1973 in fifteen South Patrol Division beats, matched on crime, calls for service, ethnic composition, median income and transiency, then split into five reactive beats with no preventive patrol, five control beats at the usual one car per beat, and five proactive beats at two to three times that level. Across victimization surveys and reported crime the three conditions showed no significant differences in crime, citizen attitudes, fear, response time, or satisfaction with response time. The report's cautions matter as much: it did not show visible presence can never matter in selected circumstances, it warned against reading it as a case for fewer officers, and it noted officers' noncommitted time ran to sixty percent.

Peter Greenwood and Joan Petersilia's RAND study, report R-1776-DOJ (1975), concluded that traditional investigative approaches do not significantly affect how often cases are solved, that most are solved by routine administrative procedures, that roughly half of investigative effort could be eliminated or redirected without unduly reducing effectiveness, and that apprehension rates are likelier to rise from alert patrol and citizen cooperation than from better detective work. RAND proposed restructuring investigation, including a major offenders unit, not abolishing it.

Rapid response was the third assumption to go. William Spelman and Dale Brown's 1981 study for the Police Executive Research Forum examined more than four thousand victims and witnesses in four cities and found that citizen reporting time, not police response time, most affects the chance of an on-scene arrest: shaving minutes off dispatch pays when a crime is reported as it happens and little otherwise, since most calls arrive after the offender has gone. None of these studies says police do not matter. Each says one tactic delivered less than its reputation promised.

collegeVersion.heading: What the job is actually made of
collegeVersion.body:
The most careful early measurement is Eric Scott's 1981 NIJ study, in which observers coded 26,418 citizen calls in departments across Rochester, St. Louis and Tampa-St. Petersburg into twelve categories, recording each as the caller described it. Requests for information were the largest category at twenty-one percent, nonviolent crime second at seventeen, then assistance at twelve, public nuisances at eleven, traffic at nine, interpersonal conflict at seven, and violent crime at two. Fewer than a fifth of calls concerned criminal incidents at all. Two cautions travel with those numbers: departments classify the same event differently, so category boundaries move the percentages, and the familiar claim that about eighty percent of patrol workload is noncriminal inherits that ambiguity even though studies converge on it.

Contemporary data show the same shape without settling on one number. Cynthia Lum, Christopher Koper and Xiaoyun Wu analysed millions of 911 calls across nine U.S. agencies in a 2022 Police Quarterly article and reported that the range and volume of what people call police about is very large and mostly not obviously transferable to other organisations without substantial added resources. The Bureau of Justice Statistics found from its 2022 Police-Public Contact Survey, published in October 2024, that nineteen percent of U.S. residents aged sixteen or older, about 49.2 million people, had police contact in the previous twelve months: 7.6 percent police-initiated, 11.2 percent resident-initiated, 2.5 percent from a traffic accident. Fifty-eight percent of those whose most recent contact was police-initiated were drivers in traffic stops, and forty-six percent of resident-initiated contacts were to report a possible crime. The modal encounter between an American and an officer is a traffic stop; the modal reason an American contacts police is to report something. That is a regulatory and service relationship far more often than an adversarial one - the conclusion the 1967 Commission had already reached when it wrote that officers perform a wide range of complex functions beyond serious crime.

collegeVersion.heading: Legitimacy, procedural justice, and stating the evidence honestly
collegeVersion.body:
The dominant contemporary framework for the police role is procedural justice, developed principally by the social psychologist Tom Tyler. Its claim is that people cooperate with legal authority mainly because they regard it as legitimate, and judge legitimacy from how they are treated rather than from whether they liked the outcome. The National Academies committee that reviewed proactive policing in 2018 sets out four elements: voice, the chance to state your side before a decision; neutrality, consistent and explained rule-based decisions; respect, dignified treatment; and trustworthiness, a belief that the officer's motives are benevolent.

Report that evidence at the strength it has. The committee found perceptions of procedurally just treatment strongly associated with judgements of legitimacy and willingness to cooperate, but concluded the research base was insufficient to establish that procedurally just policing causally produces either (Conclusion 6-4). On crime it found the evidence base very small: too small to conclude that procedural justice policing affects crime or disorder, and too small to conclude it does not (Conclusion 4-11). Insufficient evidence is not evidence of absence, the committee stressed, and procedural justice has stronger causal support in courts and workplaces. So: a well-supported association, a promising theory, an open causal question in policing.

Two habits carry this topic: separate event, evidence and interpretation - 1829 is an event, the Home Office note is evidence about authorship, 'policing by consent' is an interpretation - and date every finding while naming its jurisdiction. This lesson is educational material on institutional history, not legal advice, and takes no position on current policy. Police discretion, use of force, community policing and search and seizure law have their own lessons in this unit.

vocabulary.definition: A pre-modern arrangement in which townsmen, or paid substitutes, guarded streets and gates between sunset and daybreak and raised the alarm, with no full-time paid organisation behind them.
A locally appointed officeholder in English law enforcement, originally unpaid and serving by rotation, who supervised watchmen, executed warrants and answered to the justice of the peace.
The statute (1829 c. 44) that established London's first full-time uniformed force of about a thousand men under two commissioners accountable to the Home Secretary.
A nine-item statement of policing-by-consent philosophy popularly credited to Robert Peel; the Home Office says the link to him is unevidenced and points to the first commissioners instead.

An armed, legally authorised patrol created by southern colonial and state statutes to police enslaved people, with power to search dwellings, stop those travelling without a pass, and inflict punishment.
Kelling and Moore's label for roughly 1840s to early 1900s American policing, in which ward politicians supplied authority, the function was broad, and precincts operated with little central control.

Kelling and Moore's label for the professional model that took hold in the 1930s, grounding authority in law and expertise, narrowing the mission to crime control, and relying on car patrol and rapid response.

Driving or walking an assigned area at random when not answering calls, on the theory that visible presence deters offenders; the Kansas City experiment found little crime or fear effect from the marked-car version.
Requests the public makes of a police agency, usually by telephone, which together form the main measured picture of what an agency is asked to handle.
The idea that people judge an authority's legitimacy by the fairness of how they are treated, assessed through voice, neutrality, respect and perceived trustworthiness of motive.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: For most of history, keeping order was a chore your town made you take turns doing, like shovelling snow off the sidewalk. England only invented a paid, full-time, uniformed police force in 1829. Northern American cities copied it from the 1830s onward, but southern colonies had already built armed patrols to hunt down escaping enslaved people a century earlier, so the country really has two family trees, not one. Then people started measuring what police actually do all day. It turned out that driving around randomly did not lower crime much, that most cases were solved by routine paperwork and by information victims and witnesses had already supplied rather than by detective work, and that arriving fast usually did not help because the call came in too late anyway. It also turned out that most of the job is not crime at all. It is answering questions, sorting out arguments, traffic, and taking reports.
eli10.analogy: Think of a hospital emergency department. Its dramatic reputation is built on trauma cases, but most of what walks through the door is sprains, fevers, paperwork and people who are not sure where else to go. Policing is like that: the rare, serious event defines the public image while the ordinary volume defines the actual work.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy fails in the part that matters most. An emergency department cannot arrest you, search you, or use force against you, and nobody founded one to enforce a racial hierarchy. Police carry coercive legal authority in every one of those routine calls, and in some American jurisdictions the institution's ancestor was a slave patrol. Reputation versus workload is a fair comparison; power and origin are not.

workedExample: A classmate writes that 'the Kansas City experiment proved police patrol does not work, so cities should cut patrol budgets.' Test it against the report. First check what varied: three matched sets of five beats over twelve months in 1972-73, with routine preventive patrol removed, held constant, or raised to two or three times its usual level. Then check what was measured: reported crime, victimization, fear, attitudes, response time. Then check the finding: no significant differences among the three conditions. Now check the scope. The study tested one tactic, random patrol by marked car, in one city, in one year. It did not test whether police exist, whether officers answer calls, or whether targeted patrol at high-crime places works, and the authors explicitly warned that visible presence may matter in selected circumstances and that the results are not a case for fewer officers. The defensible version of your classmate's sentence is narrower: random preventive patrol showed no measurable payoff, and Kansas City found officers' noncommitted time was sixty percent, so the question worth asking is what that time should be spent on instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Attributing the nine 'Peelian principles' to Robert Peel as documented fact.
commonMistakes.correction: The Home Office's own note says there is no evidence of a link to Peel and credits the first commissioners, Rowan and Mayne, with instructions issued from 1829. Say 'the principles associated with Peel' and note the dispute.

commonMistakes.mistake: Flattening the origins question in either direction: claiming all American policing descends from slave patrols, or leaving slave patrols out of the story entirely.
commonMistakes.correction: State the documented part - southern statutes from the 1740s onward created patrols that are direct institutional ancestors in those jurisdictions - and mark the rest as an interpretive dispute among historians, alongside the traceable northern descent from the watch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the Kansas City experiment as proof that police presence never affects crime.
commonMistakes.correction: It tested random preventive patrol by marked car in one city over one year and found no significant effect on crime or fear. The report itself says this does not show that visible presence can have no impact in selected circumstances.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Kelling and Moore's three eras as a national timetable every department followed.
commonMistakes.correction: The authors call the boundaries unclear, and Williams and Murphy argue the scheme is drawn from the urban Northeast and omits how slavery and segregation shaped policing. Use it as a framework for comparing strategies, not as chronology.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reporting procedural justice research as though the causal effect on legitimacy or crime is established.
commonMistakes.correction: The 2018 National Academies review found strong associations but insufficient evidence to conclude that procedurally just policing causally raises legitimacy or cooperation, and a very small evidence base on crime effects in either direction.

compareContrast.distinction: The Act is a verifiable statute with a citation (1829 c. 44) that created an institution. The principles are a philosophy statement of disputed authorship, issued as general instructions rather than enacted, and the Home Office denies an evidenced link to Peel.

compareContrast.a: Northern municipal lineage (watch to day force to unified department)
compareContrast.distinction: Both are documented. The northern line runs from Boston's watch of 1636 to its day force in 1838 and New York's unification statute of 1844; the southern line runs from statutes such as South Carolina's in the 1740s and Georgia's in 1757. What historians dispute is not their existence but their relative weight in explaining American policing overall.

Calls data count what the public asks the agency to handle and are recorded by the agency; contact surveys ask a population sample about encounters, including police-initiated ones such as traffic stops that generate no call. They answer different questions and neither alone describes the workload.

compareContrast.a: Association between procedural justice and legitimacy
compareContrast.b: Causal effect of procedural justice policing
compareContrast.distinction: The 2018 National Academies review found the association strong and consistent, and the causal evidence in the policing context insufficient to support a conclusion either way. Reporting the first as if it were the second overstates the research.

keyTakeaway: Modern policing is a set of institutional choices with datable origins and at least two American lineages, and the measured job has always been much broader than crime fighting - so state what is documented, name what historians dispute, and date every finding you cite.

questionBank.prompt: According to the UK Home Office's published note on policing by consent, who most likely devised the nine principles commonly called the 'Peelian principles'?
options: Robert Peel, who drafted them personally before introducing the 1829 Act
Charles Rowan and Richard Mayne, the first Commissioners of Police of the Metropolis
The Royal Commission on the Police, in its 1962 final report
Parliament, which enacted them as a schedule to the Metropolitan Police Act 1829
questionBank.explanation: The Home Office note states there is no evidence of any link to Robert Peel and that the principles were likely devised by the first commissioners, Rowan and Mayne, and set out in the General Instructions issued to every new officer from 1829. That rules out option A. The 1962 Royal Commission is a much later body, and the principles were instructions to officers rather than statutory text, so they were never a schedule to the Act.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the sourced provenance of the Peelian principles and separating attribution from evidence

questionBank.prompt: The Kansas City Preventive Patrol Experiment (1972-73) compared reactive, control, and proactive beats. Which statement best describes what the summary report concluded?
options: Removing routine patrol from a beat produced large increases in reported burglary and robbery
Tripling patrol in the proactive beats cut victimization roughly in half
Routine preventive patrol by marked car showed little value for preventing crime or reducing fear, though the report warned it had not shown that visible presence can never matter
The experiment demonstrated that cities could safely employ substantially fewer officers
questionBank.explanation: The three conditions produced no significant differences in crime, citizen attitudes, fear, response time, or satisfaction, which rules out the first two options. The report states plainly that it did not show visible police presence can have no impact in selected circumstances, and it warns explicitly that the results should not be read as implying fewer officers are needed, which rules out the last option.
questionBank.skill: Stating an experimental finding together with the limits its authors placed on it

questionBank.prompt: A student writes: 'American policing began with the slave patrols.' Which revision is best supported by Williams and Murphy's 1990 NIJ paper?
options: American policing began with Boston's 1838 day force and New York's unified department; slave patrols were a separate militia matter with no policing powers
Slave patrols are the single origin of every police department in the United States

Southern colonies enacted slave patrol statutes decades before northern cities created municipal forces, and some historians argue those patrols were the earliest American modern-style policing; the conventional northern account omits them
Slave patrols existed but were purely private arrangements among plantation owners, so they fall outside the history of public policing
questionBank.explanation: Williams and Murphy present the slave-patrol origin as a strong argument attributed to Walker and Reichel, not as a settled finding, and their target is the omission of the South from the standard account. The first option denies a documented lineage; the second overstates an interpretive argument as fact; the fourth is wrong because the patrols were created by colonial and state statute with legal powers of search and punishment.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing documented event, interpretive argument, and overgeneralization in contested historiography

questionBank.prompt: A chief cites the 1975 RAND criminal investigation study to justify abolishing the detective bureau entirely. What is the most accurate response?
options: The study supports it, because RAND found that detectives essentially never solve cases

RAND found most cases are solved by routine administrative procedures and that about half of investigative effort could be cut or redirected, but it recommended restructuring investigation, including a major offenders unit, rather than eliminating it
The study examined patrol deployment rather than investigations, so it is irrelevant to the detective bureau
RAND concluded that apprehension rates rise mainly through more intensive follow-up investigation on every case
questionBank.explanation: RAND's summary report concluded that traditional investigative approaches do not significantly affect clearance rates, that most cases are solved through routine administrative procedures, and that roughly half of investigative effort could be eliminated or shifted, while proposing reforms such as reduced follow-up on minor cases, a major offenders unit, and prosecutor-supervised post-arrest investigation. It did not find detectives never solve cases, it did study investigations, and it pointed to alert patrol and citizen cooperation rather than more follow-up as the route to higher apprehension.
questionBank.skill: Applying a research finding to a policy claim without exceeding what the study concluded

questionBank.prompt: Scott's 1981 NIJ study coded 26,418 citizen calls to police. Which conclusion states the result with its proper caveat?
options: Exactly 80 percent of police work in every U.S. department is noncriminal, a figure that holds across agencies
Violent-crime calls were the largest single category at 21 percent of the total

Requests for information were the largest category at 21 percent and violent-crime calls the smallest at 2 percent, but departments classify the same incident differently, so the percentages should be read as an order of magnitude
Because fewer than 20 percent of calls concerned crime, police response time is irrelevant to every offense
questionBank.explanation: Scott's Table 3-1 puts information requests at 21 percent and violent crime at 2 percent, and the report warns repeatedly that call classification varies by department, which is why it also treats the familiar 80 percent figure as carrying that same ambiguity rather than as an exact constant. Option B inverts the data. Option D confuses this study with the response-time research, which found that fast response still matters for crimes reported while in progress.
questionBank.skill: Reading workload data accurately and carrying the study's stated measurement caveats with the number

title: Police Discretion
in30Seconds: Police discretion is an officer's authority to choose among lawful options: to stop a car or let it go, to warn or cite, to arrest or release, to charge someone or route them toward treatment. It exists because criminal codes reach far more conduct than any agency can process, budgets are finite, and statutes need judgment to apply to real situations. The live question in research and policy is not whether officers have discretion but how it is guided, recorded, and reviewed.
whyItMatters: Discretion is where the criminal justice system actually begins. Officers decide which of the many technically enforceable events become cases at all, and every later actor works from that filtered set. Understanding how discretion operates lets you read stop and search statistics carefully: neither waving away documented disparities nor treating any gap as settled proof of discrimination. It also explains why most reform proposals target written policy, supervision, data review, and oversight rather than trying to abolish judgment, which cannot be done. If you can tell a legal limit from a policy limit from an empirical finding, this literature becomes readable rather than a shouting match.
learningObjectives: Define police discretion and explain why it is a structural feature of enforcement rather than a defect in it.
Distinguish Goldstein's total enforcement, full enforcement, and no enforcement zones and locate discretion within them.
Identify the decision points at which discretion operates and the factors research associates with those decisions.
Analyze what benchmark, veil-of-darkness, outcome, and threshold tests can and cannot establish about disparity.
Evaluate mechanisms that structure discretion, including written policy, cameras, early intervention systems, and pattern-or-practice litigation.

collegeVersion.heading: Discretion is built into enforcement, not bolted onto it
collegeVersion.body: Start with a counting problem. Every jurisdiction's criminal code and traffic code together describe far more conduct than any police agency has the officers, hours, or budget to act on. Writing the law is cheap; enforcing it is not. Joseph Goldstein's 1960 article in the Yale Law Journal gave this situation a useful geometry. Total enforcement would mean acting on everything the substantive criminal law describes. Police can never reach that perimeter, because constitutional rules, statutes, and court decisions carve out a no-enforcement area in which officers have no authority to invoke the criminal process at all. What remains is the full enforcement zone: the conduct police are legally permitted to pursue. Goldstein's point was that even full enforcement is not a realistic expectation. Definitions of offenses and of procedural limits are ambiguous at the edges, and the day-to-day pressures on an agency make complete enforcement of the remainder impossible. So officers select. That selection is police discretion, and it is not an escape hatch from the law; it is the ordinary condition of applying law to a world that produces more violations than the system can absorb. This lesson describes arrangements in the United States, and it is educational material rather than legal advice. Enforcement authority, agency policy, and oversight structures vary considerably from state to state and department to department.

collegeVersion.heading: Why the widest routine discretion sits at the bottom of the organization
collegeVersion.body: Most bureaucracies concentrate discretionary authority at the top. Policing inverts that picture for routine decisions. A patrol officer working alone decides, in seconds and usually without a supervisor present, whether an encounter happens at all. Goldstein emphasized that decisions not to invoke the criminal process are of extremely low visibility: a warning issued and forgotten, a car not pulled over, a dispute settled on a sidewalk. Nothing is filed, so nothing can be reviewed. Decisions to invoke the process generate paper and therefore generate scrutiny from prosecutors, judges, and defense counsel. Non-decisions generate neither, which is why they escape the checks the rest of the system relies on. Michael Lipsky generalized this pattern in his 1980 book on street-level bureaucracy, later reissued in an expanded thirtieth anniversary edition. Frontline public servants who deal directly with the public, he argued, hold substantial discretionary authority while carrying heavy caseloads, working toward ambiguous agency goals, and operating with inadequate resources; they cope by rationing what they provide and by routinizing cases into familiar types. The routines they build become, in practice, what the agency does. Read that way, the officer on the street is not deviating from policy when she exercises judgment. She is producing the agency's real policy, one encounter at a time.

collegeVersion.heading: Where discretion operates: the decision points
collegeVersion.body: Discretion is easier to study when you break an encounter into the choices it contains. Whether to initiate contact at all. Whether to extend the contact into a search. Whether to close it with no action, a verbal or written warning, a citation, or an arrest. Whether to use force, and how much. Whether to route a person toward services rather than charges. Each choice is separately measurable, and the outcomes differ. In the Bureau of Justice Statistics' 2022 Police-Public Contact Survey, among residents age sixteen or older whose most recent police contact was as a driver in a traffic stop, about 9 percent reported no enforcement action, 44 percent a warning, 43 percent a ticket, and 4 percent a search or arrest. Those are self-reported figures from a nationally representative supplement to the National Crime Victimization Survey, not agency records, and the distinction matters when comparing them to administrative data. The referral decision is newer as a formal option. A 2026 conjoint survey experiment published in Health and Justice presented 329 officers in five agencies running pre-booking diversion programs with forced choices about whom to send to treatment instead of jail; the officers' choices tracked legal characteristics such as criminal history severity, drug quantity, and whether another offense had occurred, and also varied with the age, sex, and race of the person described.

collegeVersion.heading: What research associates with discretionary choices
collegeVersion.body: Law sets the outer boundary. Fourth Amendment doctrine on stops, searches, and warrants is the subject of a separate lesson, but its practical effect here is simple: legal rules define what an officer may do, and leave wide room inside that boundary for what an officer will do. Research on what fills that room has been running since the field observation studies of the 1960s. Complainant preference shows up early and persistently; Goldstein documented a department that declined to enforce felonious assault laws when the victim would not sign a complaint, which effectively let the complainant rather than the statute decide whether a felony was a felony. Suspect demeanor has been studied and contested for decades. Worden and Shepard's 1996 reanalysis of the Police Services Study data reported that the association between a disrespectful or hostile demeanor and arrest held up, after other researchers had questioned it. Situation matters as well. The National Academies' 2018 consensus report on proactive policing observes that where policies widen the scope for officer discretion, they may increase the potential for cues such as race to affect behavior, and it summarizes psychological work indicating that task complexity, time pressure, fatigue, and fear push people generally toward superficial cues and hunches. The committee is careful to add that most of that work is laboratory research rather than observation of officers in the field. None of these findings say that officers decide arbitrarily. They say that seriousness and evidence do not explain everything, and that the unexplained remainder is where the argument lives.

collegeVersion.heading: Measuring disparity: four tools and their limits
collegeVersion.body: Disparities in stop and search decisions are documented, and the tools for probing them are worth learning precisely. Pierson and colleagues compiled 94,778,505 traffic stops from 21 state patrol agencies and 35 municipal police departments and published the analysis in Nature Human Behaviour in 2020. The first tool is a benchmark: compare stops to some population at risk. Their per-capita figures showed black drivers stopped more often than white drivers and Hispanic drivers less often, but the authors immediately noted that residential population is a poor denominator, since it ignores time spent driving, driving behavior, and the fact that drivers often are stopped where they do not live. The second tool, the veil-of-darkness test, compares who is stopped at the same clock time in darkness versus daylight, exploiting seasonal and daylight-saving shifts. Black drivers made up a smaller share of stops after dark in both state patrol and municipal data, which the authors read as suggestive of bias in stop decisions while listing ways lighting and violation type could distort the result. The third tool is the outcome test, attributed to Becker: compare hit rates, the share of searches that find contraband. Across state patrol stops, contraband was found in 32.0 percent of searches of white drivers, 29.4 percent of black drivers, and 24.3 percent of Hispanic drivers, even though black and Hispanic drivers were searched roughly twice as often. The outcome test suffers from infra-marginality: if the underlying distributions of risk differ, one race-neutral search threshold can still yield unequal hit rates, so the test can flag bias that is not there and miss bias that is. The fourth tool, the threshold test, estimates the evidentiary bar applied to each group; the authors inferred lower thresholds for black and Hispanic drivers, while stating that thresholds are not identified by the data alone and depend on model assumptions.

collegeVersion.heading: What the disparity evidence does and does not settle
collegeVersion.body: Here the honest answer is that researchers disagree, and the disagreement is about causation rather than about the existence of the gaps. The National Academies' 2018 committee stated two conclusions directly. First, large racial disparities in the volume and nature of police-citizen encounters are likely whenever police concentrate enforcement on high-risk people or high-risk places, which many proactive strategies do by design. Second, existing evidence does not establish conclusively whether, or to what extent, those disparities reflect statistical prediction, racial animus, implicit bias, or other causes. The committee paired that with the observation that the history of racial injustice in American criminal justice, together with ethnographic work on the effects of policing in non-white communities, makes the causes a priority for research and policy. Two things follow for a student. Reporting a disparity is not the same as explaining it, and refusing to explain it is not the same as denying it. Deployment is the clearest confounder: if patrol hours are concentrated in some neighborhoods, residents there will accumulate more encounters regardless of how any individual officer decides. That is a real effect on people's lives, and it is a different mechanism from an officer treating two similar drivers differently.

collegeVersion.heading: Structuring discretion instead of pretending to remove it
collegeVersion.body: Because discretion cannot be eliminated, agencies and courts try to channel it. Written policy is the first instrument, and its coverage is uneven. Bureau of Justice Statistics data from the 2016 LEMAS survey show that 84.8 percent of local police departments had a written directive on motor-vehicle stops and 71.3 percent had one on stop and frisk; because large agencies are likelier to have policies, those directives covered 95.6 percent and 85.7 percent of officers respectively. Training and supervision are the second instrument, and the Justice Department's 2017 findings report on the Chicago Police Department illustrates what investigators look for: supervisor span of control, whether supervisors work consistently with the same officers, and whether anyone reviews what officers actually do. Recording technology is the third. By 2016, 47 percent of the country's 15,328 general-purpose agencies had acquired body-worn cameras, and about 86 percent of adopters had a formal camera policy. The evidence that cameras change behavior is mixed: the National Institute of Justice reports that a review of 70 studies found no consistent or no statistically significant effects, earning a No Effects rating from CrimeSolutions across use of force, arrests, stops, and complaints, while individual evaluations range from Effective in Boston to No Effects in Washington, D.C. Early intervention systems are the fourth. As the Justice Department described them in the Chicago report, such a system tracks officer conduct, flags risk of future problems, and triggers non-disciplinary responses such as additional training or counseling; Chicago's, the Department found, existed in name only.

collegeVersion.heading: Accountability structures and their legal limits
collegeVersion.body: Four accountability mechanisms are worth distinguishing. Internal investigation is the baseline: in 2016, 88.4 percent of local police departments had a written directive on investigating employee misconduct. External criminal investigation requirements are separate and uneven; 59.4 percent of departments required an outside law enforcement body to investigate a firearm discharged at a person, and 82.6 percent required one when force caused death, though those requirements were markedly less common in the largest agencies, and the BJS question excluded civilian review. Civilian oversight bodies sit outside the agency and form a third layer; they are created locally, and the BJS figures just cited say nothing about them, because the survey question expressly excluded civilian reviews. Fourth is federal structural litigation. Under 34 U.S.C. section 12601, enacted as part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994 and originally codified at 42 U.S.C. section 14141, it is unlawful for a governmental authority to engage in a pattern or practice of law enforcement conduct that deprives people of federal rights, and the Attorney General may sue for equitable and declaratory relief to eliminate it. The Civil Rights Division notes that a single incident is usually not enough, that it cannot investigate federal agencies, and that its settlements typically require data collection, independent oversight, force review, and better training and supervision. Individual damages run on a different track: 42 U.S.C. section 1983 allows suit against officials acting under color of state law, but in Harlow v. Fitzgerald (1982) the Supreme Court held that officials performing discretionary functions are shielded unless their conduct violated clearly established rights a reasonable person would have known, and in Pearson v. Callahan (2009) it held unanimously that courts may address that clearly-established question first without deciding whether a right was violated at all. Described as doctrine and nothing more, qualified immunity means many suits over discretionary decisions end on that question rather than on the merits.

vocabulary.definition: The lawful authority of an officer to choose among permissible courses of action in a given encounter, including the option of taking no formal action at all.
Goldstein's term for the zone of conduct that police are legally permitted to pursue once constitutional, statutory, and procedural limits have been subtracted from the whole criminal code.
A choice, typically not to invoke the criminal process, that leaves no record and therefore cannot be reviewed by prosecutors, courts, or supervisors.
Lipsky's term for public agencies whose frontline workers deal directly with the public, hold wide practical judgment, and effectively make agency policy through their routines.
The difficulty of choosing a defensible comparison population when judging whether a group is stopped or searched disproportionately.
An analytic method comparing the racial composition of drivers stopped at the same clock time in darkness versus daylight, on the theory that darkness obscures a driver's race.
An analytic method that compares the share of searches yielding contraband across groups, treating a lower success rate as a sign that a lower evidentiary bar was applied.
The reason success-rate comparisons can mislead: when two groups have different underlying risk distributions, a single race-neutral decision threshold still produces unequal success rates.
A federal civil inquiry under 34 U.S.C. 12601 into whether an agency systematically deprives people of federal rights, resolvable by court-enforceable equitable relief rather than damages.
A judicially created defense shielding officials sued for damages over discretionary acts unless the conduct violated clearly established law a reasonable person would have known.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine writing down every rule you would like people to follow in a city, then hiring far too few people to watch for all of it. The people you hired will have to pick what they act on. They are not cheating when they pick. Picking is the job. But once you notice that picking is the job, some questions get sharper. Which picks get written down and which vanish? Who checks the ones nobody wrote down? If two people do the same thing and get different results, is that because the situations differed, because the officers differed, or because one neighborhood gets watched more closely than another? Researchers have built careful statistical tools to attack that last question, and the tools are genuinely good, and they still cannot fully settle it.
eli10.analogy: Think of a lifeguard at a crowded public pool. The posted rules forbid running, glass bottles, diving in the shallow end, and breath-holding contests. If she blew the whistle for every violation she would never stop whistling, and she would miss the child actually going under. So she chooses. What she consistently whistles for, and what she consistently lets slide, becomes the pool's real rulebook, no matter what the sign says.
eli10.analogyLimits: The comparison breaks down in ways worth naming. A lifeguard cannot arrest anyone, cannot search a bag, and carries no weapon; the worst outcome of her judgment is usually an argument. Her decisions are not governed by constitutional law, no court reviews her whistle, and no statute authorizes a federal lawsuit over how she manages the shallow end. Police discretion carries consequences that reach into liberty and life, which is exactly why so much machinery has been built around it.

workedExample: An officer clocks a car ten miles per hour over the limit at 9 p.m. and stops it. That single stop contains at least four separable decisions. First, whether to stop at all, since many similar cars pass unstopped. Second, whether the encounter stays a conversation or extends into a search, which requires a legal basis. Third, the outcome: nothing, a warning, a ticket, or an arrest. Fourth, whether anything is written down. Using the 2022 Police-Public Contact Survey, the aggregate answer to the third question was about 9 percent no action, 44 percent warning, 43 percent ticket, and 4 percent search or arrest. Now break those outcomes out by race, as BJS does: 49.0 percent of white drivers reported a warning versus 34.7 percent of black drivers and 35.9 percent of Hispanic drivers, while 8.6 percent of black drivers reported a search or arrest versus 3.1 percent of white drivers. Those are self-reports, they are one year, and they do not control for stop reason, location, or driving record. They tell you the outcomes differ. Deciding why requires the veil-of-darkness, outcome, and threshold tools, and even those leave the causal question open.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating discretion as a loophole or an abuse to be eliminated.
commonMistakes.correction: Discretion follows from a criminal code broader than any agency's capacity and from statutes that require judgment to apply. The realistic policy question is how to structure and review it, not how to remove it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a raw stop-rate or search-rate gap as proof of discrimination.
commonMistakes.correction: Raw rates depend on the benchmark you pick. Residential population ignores driving exposure and deployment patterns, which is why researchers built the veil-of-darkness, outcome, and threshold tests instead of stopping at the raw numbers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Concluding that equal hit rates prove searches were unbiased.
commonMistakes.correction: That is the infra-marginality problem. Groups with different underlying risk distributions can produce equal or unequal hit rates under one identical, race-neutral threshold, so hit rates alone settle neither direction.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming body-worn cameras have been shown to reliably change officer behavior.
commonMistakes.correction: NIJ reports the evidence is mixed; a review of 70 studies found no consistent or no statistically significant effects, while individual city evaluations range from Effective to No Effects.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the different accountability tracks with one another.
commonMistakes.correction: Section 1983 damages suits target individuals and can end on qualified immunity; 34 U.S.C. 12601 gives the Attorney General a civil action for equitable relief against an agency's pattern or practice and cannot recover damages or prosecute anyone.

compareContrast.distinction: Discretion is the authority to choose among lawful options. Discrimination is choosing on a prohibited basis. Every discriminatory decision is an exercise of discretion, but the overwhelming majority of discretionary decisions are not discriminatory, so demonstrating discretion demonstrates nothing about bias.

The outcome test compares how often searches succeed and is vulnerable to infra-marginality. The threshold test uses a Bayesian model to estimate the evidentiary bar applied to each group from search and hit rates together, which addresses infra-marginality but makes the result depend on model form and priors.

Section 1983 lets an injured individual sue an official for damages, where qualified immunity applies. Section 12601 lets the Attorney General sue a government for equitable and declaratory relief to end a pattern or practice; it produces institutional change, not compensation.

Internal affairs sits inside the agency and reports through its chain of command; civilian oversight sits outside it. BJS's 2016 survey asked only about external investigations by another law enforcement or criminal investigative body and expressly excluded civilian reviews, so those national figures tell you nothing about how common or how empowered civilian oversight bodies are.

keyTakeaway: Discretion is the ordinary condition of enforcing a criminal code broader than any agency's capacity, and it concentrates at the lowest rank where it is least visible. The serious work is in structuring and reviewing it, and in reading disparity evidence for exactly what it measures.

questionBank.prompt: What term did Joseph Goldstein use in 1960 for police decisions not to invoke the criminal process?
options: Low-visibility decisions
Discretionary arrests
Selective incapacitation
Procedural default
questionBank.explanation: Goldstein argued that non-enforcement decisions are of extremely low visibility and are therefore seldom reviewed, unlike decisions to invoke the process, which generate records that prosecutors and courts examine. The other three options are real terms from other contexts and none names this idea.
questionBank.skill: Recall the classic term for unreviewable non-enforcement decisions

questionBank.prompt: Why did Goldstein conclude that full enforcement is not a realistic expectation?
options: Because officers are legally forbidden to enforce most of the criminal code
Because offense and procedural definitions are ambiguous at the edges and agencies face limits and pressures that preclude enforcing the remainder
Because prosecutors, not police, decide which laws are enforced
Because most criminal statutes had been formally repealed by 1960
questionBank.explanation: Goldstein placed full enforcement inside the perimeter of total enforcement, after subtracting the no-enforcement area created by constitutional and procedural limits, and then argued that ambiguity plus practical limitations make even that narrower zone unreachable. Officers are not forbidden to enforce most of the code, the article is specifically about police rather than prosecutorial choice, and it expressly set aside obsolete unrepealed laws.
questionBank.skill: Explain the structural origin of discretion

questionBank.prompt: Searches of one group turn up contraband as often as searches of another. What does the outcome test alone establish about bias in those search decisions?
options: It proves the same evidentiary bar was applied to both groups
It proves a lower bar was applied to the group searched more often
It is not decisive, because different underlying risk distributions can produce equal or unequal success rates under a single race-neutral threshold
It is not decisive, because contraband discovery is never recorded accurately
questionBank.explanation: This is infra-marginality, the standard limitation of the outcome test: with different risk distributions, one identical threshold can yield unequal hit rates and a genuinely different threshold can yield equal ones, so the test can both flag bias that is absent and miss bias that is present. The measurement-error option is not the problem the literature identifies here.
questionBank.skill: Evaluate the inferential limits of the outcome test

questionBank.prompt: A city agrees to a court-enforceable settlement requiring new data collection, independent oversight, and revised force review after a federal investigation. Which authority is most likely behind it?
options: A 42 U.S.C. 1983 damages action brought by an injured individual
A federal criminal prosecution of the officers involved
A qualified immunity ruling under Harlow v. Fitzgerald
A pattern-or-practice action under 34 U.S.C. 12601 brought by the Attorney General
questionBank.explanation: Section 12601 authorizes the Attorney General to seek equitable and declaratory relief to eliminate a pattern or practice, and the Civil Rights Division reports that its settlements commonly require data collection, independent oversight, force review, and improved training and supervision. Section 1983 produces damages for an individual rather than institutional relief, a criminal prosecution punishes people rather than reforming an agency, and qualified immunity is a defense, not a source of remedies.
questionBank.skill: Match an observed remedy to the legal authority that produces it

questionBank.prompt: A student writes that the National Academies' 2018 proactive policing report proved racial disparities in police encounters are caused by officer bias. What is the accurate correction?
options: The report concluded such disparities are likely where enforcement is concentrated, but that existing evidence does not conclusively establish whether or how much they reflect statistical prediction, animus, implicit bias, or other causes
The report concluded that no racial disparities in police encounters exist once deployment is controlled for
The report concluded that implicit bias is the primary established cause of the disparities
The report declined to address racial disparities at all
questionBank.explanation: Conclusion 7-1 states that large disparities are likely when police target high-risk people or places, and Conclusion 7-2 states that the evidence does not conclusively establish the causes, while calling those causes a key research and policy concern. The report neither denies the disparities, nor names a settled cause, nor stays silent.
questionBank.skill: State a consensus finding accurately without overreading it

quickCheck.prompt: Why did Goldstein conclude that full enforcement is not a realistic expectation?
options: Because officers are legally forbidden to enforce most of the criminal code
Because offense and procedural definitions are ambiguous at the edges and agencies face limits and pressures that preclude enforcing the remainder
Because prosecutors, not police, decide which laws are enforced
Because most criminal statutes had been formally repealed by 1960
quickCheck.explanation: Goldstein placed full enforcement inside the perimeter of total enforcement, after subtracting the no-enforcement area created by constitutional and procedural limits, and then argued that ambiguity plus practical limitations make even that narrower zone unreachable. Officers are not forbidden to enforce most of the code, the article is specifically about police rather than prosecutorial choice, and it expressly set aside obsolete unrepealed laws.
quickCheck.skill: Explain the structural origin of discretion

quickCheck.prompt: Searches of one group turn up contraband as often as searches of another. What does the outcome test alone establish about bias in those search decisions?
options: It proves the same evidentiary bar was applied to both groups
It proves a lower bar was applied to the group searched more often
It is not decisive, because different underlying risk distributions can produce equal or unequal success rates under a single race-neutral threshold
It is not decisive, because contraband discovery is never recorded accurately
quickCheck.explanation: This is infra-marginality, the standard limitation of the outcome test: with different risk distributions, one identical threshold can yield unequal hit rates and a genuinely different threshold can yield equal ones, so the test can both flag bias that is absent and miss bias that is present. The measurement-error option is not the problem the literature identifies here.
quickCheck.skill: Evaluate the inferential limits of the outcome test
