title: What Causes Crime?
in30Seconds: Criminology has no single answer to what causes crime. It has families of theories that explain different things at different levels: individual choice, the immediate situation, the neighborhood, and the wider social structure. Some are well supported for particular offenses and populations; none explains crime in general. This lesson sets up the vocabulary the rest of the unit uses and the evidence standards that separate a tested theory from a plausible story.
whyItMatters: Every crime policy carries a theory inside it, stated or not. Longer sentences assume deterrence works through severity. Targeted patrol assumes it works through certainty. Employment programs assume adult social bonds change behavior. Courses in criminology, sociology, public policy, and law all ask you to name the theory behind a claim and then ask what evidence would test it. Building that habit here - separating what a theory predicts from what the available data can actually show - is what keeps the rest of this unit from becoming a list of names to memorize, and what lets you read a crime statistic in the news without being led by it.
learningObjectives: Define a criminological theory and state what kind of evidence would count for or against one.
Distinguish individual, situational, community, and structural levels of explanation, and explain why theories at different levels are not automatically rivals.
Explain the classical school's deterrence framework and summarize the finding that certainty of apprehension deters more than severity of punishment, including its stated limits.
Describe positivist and biosocial approaches non-deterministically, and explain why the history of biological determinism requires explicit caution.
Analyze a causal claim about crime by identifying confounding, reciprocal causation, and the research designs that address them.

collegeVersion.heading: What a criminological theory is, and what would count as evidence
collegeVersion.body:
The American Society of Criminology describes its members as pursuing knowledge about the measurement, etiology, consequences, prevention, control, and treatment of crime and delinquency. Etiology means causation, so this lesson's question is a defining object of the discipline.

A criminological theory is not a hunch about why people offend. It is a general explanation that names its concepts, states how they relate, and predicts specifically enough to be shown wrong. The working standard is the ordinary standard of social science: a theory must be falsifiable; its concepts must be operationalized, meaning translated into something measurable; and researchers must rule out spuriousness, where two things move together only because a third is moving both. Ice cream sales and murder rates rise together, and nobody thinks the ice cream is doing the work.

What counts as evidence, then, is not a memorable case. A theory gains support when its predictions hold across independent samples, across different measures of the same concept, and against designs that make competing explanations implausible. It loses support when the relationship vanishes once a plausible confounder is controlled, or when it holds for one offense type but not the others it claims to cover. Theories are therefore supported for particular offenses and particular populations, not universally. No single theory explains crime.

collegeVersion.heading: Four levels of explanation, and why they are not automatically rivals
collegeVersion.body:
Explanations of crime operate at different scales. An individual-level account asks why this person and not that one; a situational account asks why this moment, this target, this place; a community-level account asks why offending concentrates in some neighborhoods; a structural account asks why rates differ across societies, eras, and social positions. Criminology texts draw much the same distinction as macro versus micro: macro-level explanations address group rate differences and point toward social structures, while micro-level explanations address differences among individuals and point toward social processes.

Levels change what a theory is answering. "Why did this burglary happen?" and "Why does this city have a higher burglary rate than that one?" are different questions, and an answer to one is not automatically an answer to the other. So theories at different levels need not be competitors: a structural account of how opportunity is distributed and an individual account of who takes an available opportunity can both hold. They become rivals only when they predict different things about the same outcome, measured the same way, in the same population.

collegeVersion.heading: The classical school and deterrence
collegeVersion.body:
Modern deterrence theory descends from two Enlightenment writers. Cesare Beccaria published Dei delitti e delle pene - On Crimes and Punishments - in 1764, attacking cruel and arbitrary treatment of the accused and arguing that penalties should be proportioned to harm, set by legislatures, and applied equally. Jeremy Bentham, the English utilitarian, held that punishment must be justified by its effects. The 2014 National Research Council review summarizes their shared framework: deterrence has three ingredients - severity, certainty, and celerity, or swiftness - and severity alone cannot deter, because a penalty unlikely to arrive threatens little. Beccaria thought probability mattered more than cruelty.

Research has largely borne that out, and it is the most policy-relevant empirical result in the unit. The National Institute of Justice's summary of the deterrence literature states that the certainty of being caught is a vastly more powerful deterrent than the punishment; that increasing severity does little to deter, partly because people know very little about the sanctions attached to specific crimes; and that police deter chiefly by strengthening the perception that offenders will be caught. The National Research Council reached the same place from the sentencing side, concluding that the incremental deterrent effect of increases in already-lengthy prison sentences is modest at best.

The NRC adds a qualification that is easy to lose: essentially all the evidence on certainty concerns the certainty of apprehension, not the certainty of imprisonment once a person is convicted. Keep one more distinction straight. Deterrence is a person not yet caught deciding not to offend; incapacitation is a confined person being unable to offend.

collegeVersion.heading: Positivism, biology, and a history that has to be named
collegeVersion.body:
Where the classical school assumed a free and calculating chooser, positivism assumed that offending has measurable causes. Positivism in this sense is a commitment to measurement, objectivity, and causal inference, and that commitment is now simply how criminology works. Its early substantive content, however, was largely wrong and did severe harm.

Cesare Lombroso, an Italian physician, published the first edition of Criminal Man in 1876 and claimed that a large share of offenders were born criminals - evolutionary throwbacks identifiable by physical features. Kaufmann and Vestad document the method: the book opens with cranial measurements of sixty-six skulls sorted by circumference, offered as proof that criminal skulls were abnormal. Charles Goring later added claimed mental deficiencies, and in the United States H. H. Goddard used intelligence testing to sort people for institutionalization, deportation, or sterilization.

This was not a fringe. The National Human Genome Research Institute records that eugenics - the scientifically erroneous theory that humans can be improved by selective breeding - drew popular, elite, and governmental support in many countries, and that at least 60,000 people were involuntarily sterilized under thirty states' laws by the 1970s, disproportionately Latinx, Native American, African American, poor white, and disabled people. In Buck v. Bell, 274 U.S. 200 (1927), the Supreme Court upheld Virginia's compulsory sterilization statute over a lone dissent, and Justice Holmes wrote for the Court that society may prevent the manifestly unfit from reproducing rather than wait "to execute degenerate offspring for crime." A hereditary theory of crime was written into American constitutional law.

Contemporary biosocial criminology is a different enterprise and must not be described in the old vocabulary. There is no crime gene. Research reports modest correlations between certain genetic variants, neurochemical and hormonal measures, and antisocial behavior - correlations whose direction is often unclear, since testosterone rises after aggressive behavior as well as before it, and whose effects depend heavily on environment. Anything stronger than a conditional, probabilistic statement goes past the evidence, and the paragraph above is what stronger statements have been used for.

collegeVersion.heading: Psychological approaches
collegeVersion.body:
Psychological accounts locate causes in relatively stable individual differences: personality, self-regulation, cognition, development. Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck concluded from mid-century data that there is no single criminal personality; later work found instead a cluster of interrelated traits correlated with offending, including impulsivity, low self-control, low empathy, and difficulty learning from punishment. The Southern Oregon criminology text reports Caspi and colleagues (1994) finding two broad traits, constraint and negative emotionality, to be robust correlates of delinquency.

None of these traits is criminal in itself, and most people who score high on them never offend. Treat a personality correlate as you would any risk factor: it shifts a probability across a population and predicts very little about a particular person - which is true of nearly every correlate in this field.

collegeVersion.heading: Social structure and social process: the two families
collegeVersion.body:
Most of contemporary criminology sorts into two families, and the rest of this unit is organized around them. Social-structural theories ask why crime rates differ across groups, places, and periods, and look to how a society distributes opportunity, disadvantage, and collective capacity. Social-process theories ask how a particular person comes to offend, and look to learning, attachment, control, and official reaction.

Here is the map, one sentence each, because each has its own lesson. Strain theory, following Merton in 1938, argues that a disjunction between culturally promoted goals and the legitimate means available for reaching them produces pressure toward crime. Social disorganization, from Shaw and McKay's Chicago research, treats crime as a product of neighborhoods whose social institutions have lost the capacity to regulate behavior. Social learning theory, in Edwin Sutherland's differential association, holds that criminal behavior is learned in interaction within intimate personal groups. Labeling theory examines the social construction of crime and how being labeled and treated as a criminal shapes what a person does next. Routine activity theory moves the question off offenders entirely: an offense occurs when a motivated offender and a suitable target converge in time and space without a capable guardian, as Cohen and Felson argued in 1979. They sit at different levels - two mainly structural, two mainly processual, one situational - which is why they are as often complementary as competing.

collegeVersion.heading: The age-crime curve and desistance
collegeVersion.body:
One regularity here is about as solid as anything criminology has. Offending rises through late childhood, peaks in the teenage years - NIJ puts the peak at roughly ages fifteen to nineteen - and declines through the twenties and beyond. NIJ calls this bell shape universal in Western populations while noting real variation inside it: violence peaks later than property crime, girls peak earlier than boys, and the curve is higher and wider for young men in the most disadvantaged neighborhoods. NIJ's deterrence summary reports a steep decline at about age thirty-five, and the National Research Council notes that even highly active career offenders typically desist in their thirties - one reason selective incapacitation is hard to implement, since high-rate offenders are easy to identify in retrospect and hard to identify in advance.

What the curve means has been argued about for forty years. Travis Hirschi and Michael Gottfredson put the relationship at the centre of criminological theory in "Age and the Explanation of Crime" in 1983; NIJ's 2021 desistance volume records their position that longitudinal data were unnecessary because the pattern held across time and place, against the criminal-career researchers' insistence that following the same people over time was essential. Eleanor and Sheldon Glueck had already run some of the first longitudinal panels in criminology, following the same men over decades and showing that behavior improves over time even among serious offenders. Robert Sampson and John Laub - whom NIJ calls pioneers of life-course criminology - extended that tradition, defining desistance in their 2003 work as the absence of new arrests up to age seventy.

That work is why desistance is now treated as a process rather than an event. NIJ, citing Laub and Sampson, summarizes the sociological side of the literature as pointing to common life events such as stable employment and marriage, and NIJ's study-group review reports strong evidence that for males marriage and stable work foster desistance while unstructured time with peers is associated with persistence. One caution matters especially: desistance can be underway while offending is still occurring, which is why NIJ urges measuring criminality - the propensity - and not only behavior.

collegeVersion.heading: Correlation, causation, and why research design carries the weight
collegeVersion.body:
Almost every interesting claim about crime begins as a correlation, and the correlations are nearly all confounded, reciprocal, or both. Places with more police record more crime partly because police are what record crime. Incarceration rates respond to crime rates at the same time crime rates may respond to incarceration. The National Research Council makes the point directly about state panel studies: how much incarceration reduces crime depends on how strongly incarceration rates themselves depend on crime rates, and after weighing that literature the committee concluded it could not arrive at a precise estimate, or even a modest range of estimates, of incarceration's effect on crime. That is a striking result for one of the field's most studied questions, and a warning about the rest.

So design carries the weight. Randomized experiments, natural experiments in which exposure is assigned by something unrelated to the outcome, and longitudinal panels following the same people or places over time are what let a criminologist argue for causation rather than association - and why the age-crime debate turned, since a cross-sectional snapshot cannot distinguish a population aging out from individuals changing.

The same discipline is required when the variables are income or race, and what is measured should be stated. In the 2023 National Crime Victimization Survey, the violent victimization rate was 39.0 per 1,000 persons age twelve or older in households earning under $25,000, against 15.7 per 1,000 in households earning $200,000 or more; it was 26.9 per 1,000 for non-Hispanic Black respondents and 22.5 for non-Hispanic white respondents, against a national rate of 22.5. But measurement is not neutral. Police-generated statistics are shaped by where police are deployed, and the National Academies' 2018 proactive policing report concluded that large racial disparities in police-citizen encounters are likely wherever police concentrate on high-risk people or places, and that existing evidence does not conclusively establish whether those disparities indicate statistical prediction, racial animus, implicit bias, or other causes. Report the measured differences, name the measurement problem, and do not present a causal account of them as settled. Recorded crime is not total crime either: BJS states that the system does not respond to most crime because so much is never reported, and the FBI's 2023 national figures rest on voluntary agency submissions.

collegeVersion.heading: What follows for policy, and what does not
collegeVersion.body:
A theory, even a well-supported one, does not hand you a policy. The deterrence research supports raising the perceived certainty of apprehension - but which agency does that, at what cost, by what methods, with what effect on the people policed, and with what consent from the community are separate questions no deterrence finding answers. Values enter where the evidence stops, and honest analysis marks that line.

This lesson is educational material about criminology and the United States criminal justice system. It is not legal advice and takes no position on any policy question. Crime is defined and measured under state as well as federal law, and both vary by jurisdiction.

vocabulary.definition: A general, testable explanation of offending that names its concepts, states how they relate, and predicts specifically enough to be shown wrong.
The scale at which an account operates - a single person, an immediate situation, a neighborhood, or an entire social structure.
Prevention of offending by the threat of sanction, analyzed by classical writers through severity, certainty, and swiftness.
The probability that someone who commits an offense is actually caught, which research identifies as the strongest sanction-based influence on offending.
Prevention of offending by removing the physical ability to offend, as when a person is confined.
The commitment to studying behavior through measurement, systematic observation, and causal inference rather than assumption.
Research on how biological measures interact with social environments to shift the probability of antisocial behavior, treating neither as destiny.
The bell-shaped pattern in which offending rises in late childhood, peaks in the teenage years, and declines through adulthood.
The process by which a person's offending and underlying propensity decline over time, distinguished from a single moment of stopping.
The situation in which two variables appear related only because a third variable is driving both of them.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Start with an easier question: what causes a car crash? A crash investigator will not accept one answer. The driver was tired. The tire was bald. The curve was banked badly and the streetlight was out. The county has not funded road maintenance in nine years. Every one of those is a real cause, they sit at different levels, and none of them becomes false because the others are true. Crime works the same way. Some explanations are about a person, some about a moment, some about a place, and some about how a whole society is arranged. Criminologists also insist on the thing a good investigator insists on: showing that a suspected cause actually did the work, rather than merely happening to be nearby.
eli10.analogy: Studying the causes of crime is like running a crash investigation: you gather what happened, list every candidate cause at every level, and then try to knock candidates out - instead of falling in love with the first explanation that sounds convincing.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks in two places. A crash investigator studies one event and can often reconstruct it in detail, while criminologists mostly study rates across thousands of people and can rarely explain any single act. And a crash has physical causes you can inspect, while crime is defined by law: change the statute and the same behavior stops being a crime, which is not something any legislature can do to a collision.

workedExample: A state legislature considers two bills. Bill A raises the maximum sentence for residential burglary from ten years to twenty. Bill B funds targeted patrol on the twenty blocks where burglary reports concentrate. Apply the evidence rather than intuition. Bill A operates on severity, and NIJ's summary of the deterrence literature reports that increasing severity does little to deter, partly because people rarely know the sentencing exposure for a given offense; the 2014 National Research Council review found the incremental deterrent effect of increases in already-lengthy sentences to be modest at best. Bill B operates on the perceived certainty of apprehension, which the same research identifies as the more powerful channel. That analysis supports a prediction about deterrence, and then it stops. It says nothing about Bill B's cost, its effect on the residents of those twenty blocks, or whether the legislature values incapacitation or retribution enough to prefer Bill A regardless. Marking where the evidence ends is part of the answer, not a hedge.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating theories at different levels as competitors, so that accepting a structural explanation means rejecting an individual one.
commonMistakes.correction: Ask what each theory is explaining. A theory about why rates differ across neighborhoods and a theory about which individuals offend answer different questions, and they conflict only when they predict different things about the same outcome in the same population.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a correlation between a factor and crime as evidence that the factor causes crime.
commonMistakes.correction: Ask what else could produce the association: a confounder driving both, reverse causation, or measurement shaped by enforcement. The National Research Council could not even bound the size of incarceration's effect on crime for exactly this reason.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reasoning that because punishment deters, harsher punishment deters more.
commonMistakes.correction: The evidence separates certainty from severity. NIJ reports that certainty of being caught is the powerful lever and that increasing severity does little; the NRC adds that the certainty evidence concerns apprehension, not the probability of imprisonment after conviction.

commonMistakes.mistake: Describing modern biosocial research in born-criminal terms, or dismissing biology entirely because Lombroso was wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: State it conditionally. There is no crime gene; research reports modest correlations with unclear causal direction that are strongly moderated by environment. That is neither the old determinism nor a claim that biology is irrelevant.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the age-crime curve as an explanation rather than a finding.
commonMistakes.correction: The curve describes a pattern; it does not say why offending falls. Life-course research points to social bonds and life events, and NIJ stresses that desistance is a process that can be underway while offending continues.

compareContrast.distinction: The classical school starts from a free, calculating chooser and asks how sanctions change the calculation; positivism starts from the premise that offending has measurable causes and asks what they are. Positivism's method survived; its early biological content did not.

Deterrence prevents crime by changing the decisions of people who are not confined; incapacitation prevents crime by removing the ability to offend from people who are. A sentence can incapacitate effectively while deterring poorly, which is precisely what the NRC found for long sentences.

Certainty is the probability the sanction arrives; severity is how heavy it is. Research supports certainty - specifically certainty of apprehension - as the stronger deterrent, and finds little deterrent return to raising severity.

Structural theories explain differences in rates across groups, places, and eras through the distribution of opportunity and disadvantage; process theories explain how a given individual comes to offend through learning, attachment, control, and reaction.

A cross-sectional snapshot shows how offending varies across ages at one moment; a longitudinal panel follows the same people over time. Only the second can distinguish a population aging out from individuals actually changing, which is why the age-crime debate turned on it.

keyTakeaway: There is no single cause of crime and no single theory that explains it: criminology offers explanations at different levels, each supported for particular offenses and populations, and the work of the field is separating causes from correlations well enough that a policy conclusion could be drawn - which the theory itself never draws for you.

questionBank.prompt: According to the National Institute of Justice's summary of the deterrence literature, which feature of punishment does the research identify as the more powerful deterrent?
options: The severity of the sentence, because longer sentences raise the expected cost of offending.
The certainty of being caught, which NIJ calls a vastly more powerful deterrent than the punishment itself.
The publicity given to a sentence, because deterrence works only through news coverage.
The availability of capital punishment, which NIJ reports as the strongest single deterrent.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the central empirical finding of deterrence research
questionBank.explanation: NIJ states that the chance of being caught is a vastly more effective deterrent than even draconian punishment, and that increasing severity does little to deter partly because people know little about the sanctions attached to specific crimes. NIJ separately reports that research on capital punishment is uninformative about whether it raises, lowers, or does not affect homicide rates. Publicity is not the identified mechanism; perceived certainty of apprehension is.

questionBank.prompt: Why are a structural explanation of neighborhood crime rates and an individual explanation of who offends not automatically competing theories?
options: Because structural theories are always correct and individual theories are always wrong.
Because they answer questions at different levels, and only become rivals when they predict different things about the same outcome in the same population.
Because criminologists have agreed to treat all theories as equally supported.
Because individual-level theories cannot be tested empirically.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing levels of explanation from theoretical rivalry
questionBank.explanation: Macro-level accounts address group rate differences and point to social structure; micro-level accounts address differences among individuals and point to social process. Two accounts at different levels can both hold, and they conflict only when they make competing predictions about the same outcome, measured the same way, in the same population. Neither level is automatically correct, criminologists do not treat all theories as equally supported, and individual-level theories are routinely tested.

questionBank.prompt: A state legislature is choosing between raising the maximum burglary sentence from ten years to twenty and funding targeted patrol on the blocks where burglary reports concentrate. What does the deterrence research support?
options: The patrol proposal, because it operates on the perceived certainty of apprehension, the channel the research identifies as more powerful.
The sentence increase, because the National Research Council found large deterrent returns from lengthening long sentences.
Neither, because research has shown that criminal sanctions have no effect on behavior at all.
Both equally, since deterrence research treats severity and certainty as interchangeable.
questionBank.skill: Applying the certainty-versus-severity finding to a policy comparison
questionBank.explanation: NIJ reports that police deter crime by strengthening the perception that offenders will be caught, and that increasing severity does little to deter; the National Research Council concluded that the incremental deterrent effect of increases in already-lengthy sentences is modest at best. Sanctions are not without effect, and severity and certainty are not interchangeable - that asymmetry is the finding. Note also what the research does not decide: cost, method, community impact, and whether the legislature values incapacitation or retribution enough to prefer the sentence bill anyway.

questionBank.prompt: The National Research Council reviewed decades of state panel studies and still declined to give even a modest range of estimates for how much incarceration reduces crime. What does that outcome best illustrate?
options: That statistical methods are useless in criminology and qualitative work should replace them.
That incarceration has been proven to have no effect on crime rates.
That when a suspected cause and its outcome each respond to the other, estimating a causal magnitude is very hard, which is why research design carries so much weight.
That the committee lacked access to the relevant data.
questionBank.skill: Diagnosing reciprocal causation and its consequences for inference
questionBank.explanation: The committee's difficulty was that incarceration rates themselves depend on crime rates at the same time crime rates may depend on incarceration, so the estimated effect turns on assumptions about that dependence. The committee reviewed the panel literature rather than lacking it, and concluded that panel studies on balance support some crime reduction of uncertain magnitude - not that the effect is zero, and not that quantitative methods are useless. The lesson is that designs which break the reciprocal loop are what allow causal claims.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement accurately describes the relationship between early biological positivism and contemporary biosocial research on antisocial behavior?
options: Contemporary biosocial research has confirmed Lombroso's claim that offenders are identifiable by physical features.
Both bodies of work treat offending as biologically determined, differing only in the instruments used.
Contemporary biosocial research has established that genetic variants cause offending independent of environment.

Early biological positivism claimed inherited traits identified criminals and fed eugenic sterilization policy upheld in Buck v. Bell, while contemporary research reports only modest, environmentally moderated correlations and identifies no crime gene.
questionBank.skill: Separating a discredited historical claim from current, non-deterministic findings
questionBank.explanation: Lombroso's 1876 Criminal Man argued that offenders were atavistic types identifiable by measurable physical features; that claim was rejected, and the broader hereditary programme supported sterilization laws under which the National Human Genome Research Institute records at least 60,000 involuntary sterilizations across thirty states by the 1970s, with the Supreme Court upholding Virginia's statute in Buck v. Bell (1927). Contemporary work reports that biology plays some role that cannot be quantified, finds no crime gene, notes unclear causal direction, and emphasizes environmental moderation - so neither determinism nor confirmation of Lombroso is accurate.

Bell (public-domain U.S. judicial text, verified against the govinfo U.S. Reports PDF). The CC BY-SA open textbook chapters and the CC BY Critical Criminology article were used for corroboration only, with no wording reused.

Bell, BJS and FBI statistical publications, a CC BY history-of-criminology article, and three open-textbook chapters used as corroboration. title: Strain Theory
in30Seconds: Strain theories explain crime as a response to pressure. Robert Merton's 1938 article put that pressure in the social structure: a culture that urges everyone toward the same success goal while handing out legitimate means unevenly. Robert Agnew's 1992 general strain theory moved it inside the person, where disliked events produce negative emotions, especially anger, and crime is one way of coping. The two versions answer different questions and have fared very differently in testing. This lesson is educational material, not legal or policy advice.
whyItMatters: Strain theory is the argument you are actually hearing whenever someone says that blocked opportunity, unfairness, or pressure produces crime. Learning it properly means learning to separate three things that get run together: what Merton claimed, what Agnew claimed, and what the studies found. Courses in criminology, sociology, and public policy will ask you to name a theory's level of analysis, state its mechanism, and say what evidence would count against it. Strain theory is an unusually good place to practise, because the same label covers a macro-sociological claim about a whole society and a social-psychological claim about one adolescent's week, and the evidence for the two is not the same.
learningObjectives: Define anomie in Durkheim's sense and explain how Merton changed the concept when he borrowed it.
Explain Merton's disjunction between cultural goals and institutionalized means, and reproduce his five modes of adaptation with the conditions he attached to them.
Distinguish Cohen's status frustration from Cloward and Ohlin's differential opportunity.
Describe Agnew's three sources of strain, the emotional mechanism, and the factors that condition whether strain produces crime.
Analyze why Mertonian strain is a structural theory while general strain theory is largely social-psychological.
Evaluate the empirical record for both versions, including how the measurement of strain affects the result.

collegeVersion.heading: Durkheim's anomie, and what Merton did to it
collegeVersion.body: Emile Durkheim used the word anomie for a state of deregulation in which established rules lose their authority. In Suicide (1897) he connected it to what he called the mal d'infini: a society normally defines what its members may legitimately want in wealth, goods, and pleasure, and when that definition fails, desires run past anything that could satisfy them and expectations stop matching reality. His subject was the moral condition of a whole society, not the decisions of particular people. Merton kept the word and kept the level of analysis, but changed the mechanism. For Durkheim, anomie is desire left unregulated. For Merton, it is a mismatch between what a culture teaches people to want and what its structure lets them reach. That substitution is the whole move, and it is worth holding onto, because the two ideas get used interchangeably and they are not the same idea.

collegeVersion.heading: Merton 1938: goals, means, and the disjunction
collegeVersion.body: "Social Structure and Anomie" appeared in the American Sociological Review in October 1938, volume 3, number 5, pages 672 to 682. Merton opened by rejecting the then-common view that deviance is biological impulse breaking through social restraint; that view, he argued, gives no account of the nonbiological conditions that produce departures from prescribed conduct. His own aim was to show how some social structures exert a definite pressure on certain people to behave nonconformingly. He separated two elements of social and cultural structure. The first is the set of culturally defined goals, purposes, and interests, which together form a frame of aspirational reference. The second is the body of institutional norms that regulate the acceptable ways of reaching those goals. When a culture places extreme emphasis on a goal such as accumulated wealth as a symbol of success, and the emotional supports for the rules of the game weaken accordingly, the pressure runs toward whatever means are technically efficient rather than whatever means are approved. Merton's illustration was competitive sport, where an exclusive focus on winning makes illegitimate but effective tactics attractive; he treated it as a small image of the wider society, and noted that the surreptitious way people break the rules shows they still know what the rules are. He was explicit that the resulting pressure is not spread evenly. Where opportunity is confined to unskilled labour and manual work is culturally stigmatized, he argued, the structural result is a strain toward innovational practices.

collegeVersion.heading: The five modes of adaptation, read carefully
collegeVersion.body: On page 676 Merton laid out five logically possible modes of adjustment or adaptation in a short table with two columns, culture goals and institutionalized means. A plus sign means acceptance, a minus sign means elimination, and a plus-or-minus means rejection combined with substitution of new goals and standards. Conformity accepts both. Innovation accepts the goals and eliminates the means. Ritualism eliminates the goals and keeps the means. Retreatism eliminates both. Rebellion rejects both and substitutes new ones, which Merton set apart on its own line as a transitional response aimed at changing the structure rather than accommodating within it. Two things are routinely lost in retelling. First, Merton wrote in the very next paragraph that people shift from one alternative to another as they move between different social activities, and that these categories describe role adjustments in specific situations, not personality as a whole. Textbooks that label the table a set of personality types are asserting something he explicitly denied. Second, the five are not of equal interest to him. Conformity, he said, is the most common and most widely diffused adaptation in every society, and retreatism the least common; his stated major concern was the illegitimacy adjustment, which is innovation - keeping the success goal while dropping the approved means of reaching it.

collegeVersion.heading: Cohen, Cloward, and Ohlin: status and opportunity
collegeVersion.body: Two mid-century books extended Merton and are usually taught with him. Albert K. Cohen's Delinquent Boys: The Culture of the Gang (1955) argued that the strain need not be economic at all. Lower-class boys are measured against middle-class standards they are poorly placed to meet, and the resulting status frustration pushes them toward a group that inverts those standards and awards status on its own terms - which was the puzzle he set out to explain: why so much juvenile offending happens in company rather than alone. Richard Cloward and Lloyd Ohlin's Delinquency and Opportunity: A Theory of Delinquent Gangs (1960), building on Cloward's 1959 American Sociological Review article, added the observation Merton had skipped: illegitimate opportunities are unequally distributed too. Blocked legitimate opportunity does not automatically produce a thief, because becoming a successful thief also requires access, contacts, and tutelage. On that premise they distinguished criminal subcultures, which offer organised illicit earning; conflict subcultures, where organised illicit earning is not available either and frustration is vented through violence; and retreatist subcultures, formed by those who fail at both the legitimate and the illegitimate route. Agnew still identified Merton, Cohen, and Cloward and Ohlin as the three models most empirical strain research relied on when he wrote in 1992.

collegeVersion.heading: Agnew 1992: general strain theory
collegeVersion.body: By the early 1990s the tradition was in retreat. Agnew's own opening in "Foundation for a General Strain Theory of Crime and Delinquency" (Criminology, volume 30, number 1, February 1992, pages 47 to 87) records that after dominating deviance research in the 1960s, strain theory came under heavy attack in the 1970s, with prominent researchers - he names Hirschi in 1969 and Kornhauser in 1978 - proposing that it be abandoned, and that although it survived, its influence was much diminished. His response was to rebuild it on material from outside criminology: stress research in medical sociology and psychology, equity and justice research in social psychology, and aggression research including recent versions of frustration-aggression. The rebuilt theory widens strain from one blocked goal to three families, each of which may be actual or anticipated: the failure to achieve positively valued goals; the removal of positively valued stimuli, such as losing a relationship or a possession; and the presentation of negatively valued or noxious stimuli, such as abuse, bullying, or victimization. Agnew also separated objective strains, disliked by most people in a group, from subjective strains, disliked by the particular person experiencing them - a distinction that matters because two people can meet the same objective circumstance and react to it differently. The mechanism is emotional. Strains generate negative emotions, anger and frustration foremost, and those emotions create pressure for corrective action. Crime is one available correction: it can produce money, discharge anger, or dull the feeling.

collegeVersion.heading: What decides whether strain becomes crime
collegeVersion.body: Because almost everyone experiences strain and most people do not respond to it with crime, the theory lives or dies on what conditions the response. Agnew answered at two levels. In 2001 he specified which strains are criminogenic: those seen as unjust, those high in magnitude, those associated with low social control, and those that create some pressure or incentive toward criminal coping in particular. A large, lasting, unfair loss that crime could plausibly repair is far more dangerous than a small, fair, irreparable one. At the level of the person, criminal coping is more likely among those with poor coping skills and resources, few conventional social supports, low social control or little to lose, and a disposition toward criminal coping - criminal associates, beliefs favourable to crime, and traits such as low constraint and negative emotionality - and in situations where the costs of offending look low and the benefits high. This is where general strain theory differs most visibly from Merton, whose account of why one person innovates and another ritualizes was comparatively thin.

collegeVersion.heading: Institutional anomie theory: the macro level returns
collegeVersion.body: Steven Messner and Richard Rosenfeld took the tradition back up to Merton's original altitude in Crime and the American Dream (1994). Their institutional anomie theory holds that culturally and structurally produced pressures to secure monetary rewards, combined with weak controls from non-economic social institutions, promote high levels of instrumental crime. The claim is not simply that a society wants money; it is that when the economy dominates the other institutions, those institutions lose the capacity to restrain the pursuit. Chamlin and Cochran tested part of this on United States state data in 1995 and reported considerable but indirect support: the effect of poverty on property crime depended on structural indicators of how far non-economic institutions could offset economic deprivation. Messner and Rosenfeld themselves applied the theory across nations to levels of criminal homicide in 1997.

collegeVersion.heading: What the evidence actually shows
collegeVersion.body: The record is uneven and worth stating precisely. For classic Mertonian strain it is poor. Burton and Cullen's 1992 review found tests yielding mixed results, with the level of support varying by how strain was operationalized and with methodological limits complicating any assessment. Part of the trouble was the measure itself: strain was usually captured indirectly as the gap between a person's aspirations and their expectations. Agnew, Cullen, Burton, Evans, and Dunaway argued in 1996 that the variable the theory actually names - dissatisfaction with one's own monetary status - had been ignored in virtually all tests, and when they measured it directly in a sample of Cincinnati adults it predicted income-generating crime and drug use, most strongly among those with criminal friends and crime-favourable beliefs, which they called qualified support unlike much previous research. Relatedly, most studies find individual economic status unrelated or only weakly related to individual offending, a result Agnew reads as a modest relationship over much of the income range that becomes substantial only for the very poor. General strain theory has done better. Agnew and White's 1992 test on 1,380 New Jersey adolescents found the three types of strain had a relatively substantial effect on delinquency and drug use, conditioned by delinquent peers and self-efficacy just as predicted, which the authors themselves described as qualified support. But the honest summary stops short of vindication. Agnew conceded in 2001 that researchers have little guidance for choosing among hundreds of candidate strains and cannot explain why only some are related to crime, so what different studies call strain differs widely and the estimates are not straightforwardly comparable. Froggio's 2007 review of the 1992 to 2003 literature still treated the theory's empirical status as an open question. Effects are generally modest; neither version is an established explanation of crime in general.

collegeVersion.heading: Structural theory, social-psychological theory, and why the difference matters
collegeVersion.body: Merton's unit of analysis is a society. He is explaining why rates of deviance differ across groups and strata from the way a culture's goals sit against its distribution of legitimate means, and individuals appear as occupants of structural positions rather than as people with histories. He said as much in closing: the paper had not tested the scheme's explanatory power against a large number of group variations in the frequency of deviant and conformist behaviour. Agnew's unit is a person. Strains are events and conditions an individual dislikes, the mechanism is that individual's emotion, and the conditioning variables are coping skills, social support, self-efficacy, temperament, and peers - which is why a reviewer can accurately call general strain theory a social-psychological interpretation of delinquency. Institutional anomie theory pulls back to the macro level again. The three are best read as answers to different questions rather than as rivals, which is also why evidence that undercuts one may leave the others standing. Strain theory has been invoked in support of very different policy programmes; this lesson describes a body of scholarship and its evidence, is educational material rather than legal advice, and takes no position among those programmes.

vocabulary.definition: A breakdown in the normative regulation of desire and conduct. Durkheim used it for a state of deregulation in which traditional rules lose their authority; Merton used it for a mismatch between a culture's goals and its distribution of legitimate means.
The ends a society teaches its members to pursue and treats as worth having, forming what Merton called a frame of aspirational reference.
The normatively approved methods a society permits for reaching its valued ends, together with the moral force attached to using them.

Merton's five-way scheme for how a person may combine acceptance or elimination of a society's ends with acceptance or elimination of its approved methods: conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism, and rebellion.
Albert Cohen's term for the pressure felt by young people who are measured against standards they are poorly placed to meet and who then seek worth in a group that keeps score differently.
Cloward and Ohlin's argument that illegitimate routes to success are unequally distributed as well, so blocked legitimate access does not by itself determine what form, if any, offending will take.
An event or condition that a person dislikes, whether because most people in that group would dislike it or because this particular person does.
Responding to a disliked event by breaking the law, rather than through the legal alternatives available to the same person.

Messner and Rosenfeld's macro-level account, in which a strong cultural push toward monetary success plus weak restraint from a society's non-economic institutions yields high rates of instrumental crime.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine a school where everyone is told that the only thing that counts is winning the science fair, and the trophy is talked about constantly. But only some students have a parent who can help, a quiet place to work, and money for materials. Merton's point is that you can predict trouble just from that setup, without knowing a single student personally. Some students will still play fair. Some will keep wanting the trophy and start cutting corners. Some will give up on the trophy but keep following every rule anyway. Some will stop caring about either. And some will try to change what the school rewards. Agnew's point is different. He says the important thing is not only the trophy but everything in a student's week that feels bad and unfair - being shoved in the hallway, losing a friend, being yelled at when you get home. Those things make people angry, anger makes people want to do something, and whether that something breaks a rule depends on who is around them and what else they know how to do.
eli10.analogy: Merton's version is like studying a game of musical chairs: you do not need to know the players to predict that people will start pushing, because the chairs were removed on purpose while the music kept telling everyone to sit down.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy stops working in three places. Musical chairs has one goal and one clear moment of failure; real strain includes losses and mistreatment that have nothing to do with any goal, which is exactly what Agnew added. In musical chairs everyone who loses knows it instantly, whereas Merton's pressure works slowly and mostly on people who never name it. And the game guarantees losers by design, while the evidence on real societies is far messier - blocked opportunity raises the odds of some kinds of offending modestly, and most people who are pushed out of the game do not push back.

workedExample: Take a seventeen-year-old who has been cut from the team he built his identity around, is being threatened daily by an older student, and has no adult he trusts enough to tell. He begins fighting at school. A Mertonian reading has little to work with here: no monetary success goal is blocked and no illegitimate earning is involved, so the case sits outside what the 1938 scheme was built to explain. Agnew's reading fits it directly. Two of the three strain types are present - the removal of something valued and the presentation of something noxious - and both are large, ongoing, and readily seen as unjust, which is the profile Agnew's 2001 criteria flag as criminogenic. The emotional pathway is anger; the conditioning factors are the absence of conventional social support and of practised legal coping. Notice what the theory does not do: it makes his fighting more probable, not predicted, and if he had one trusted adult the same strains might produce nothing at all.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Merton's five adaptations as personality types, so that a person simply is an innovator or a ritualist.
commonMistakes.correction: Merton wrote immediately after presenting the table that people shift between these alternatives across different social activities and that the categories describe role adjustments in specific situations, not personality as a whole. The same person may conform at work and innovate elsewhere.

commonMistakes.mistake: Summarising strain theory as "poverty causes crime."
commonMistakes.correction: Merton's claim is about the gap between what a culture demands and what its structure supplies, not about income by itself. Empirically, most studies find individual economic status unrelated or only weakly related to individual offending; Agnew reads the relationship as modest across most of the range and substantial only for the very poor.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading "innovation" as a compliment, or confusing it with rebellion.
commonMistakes.correction: In Merton's table innovation means keeping the culturally prescribed goal while eliminating the approved means - it is his label for the illegitimacy adjustment and his main criminological interest. Rebellion is different: it rejects both the goal and the means and substitutes new ones, aiming to change the structure rather than to succeed within it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating Agnew's general strain theory as a restatement of Merton with more examples.
commonMistakes.correction: The level of analysis changes. Merton explains rates of deviance across a society's strata from the arrangement of goals and means; Agnew explains an individual's offending through disliked events, the negative emotions they produce, and that person's coping resources and associates.

commonMistakes.mistake: Citing strain theory as a confirmed explanation of crime.
commonMistakes.correction: Tests of classic strain have been mixed, with support depending heavily on how strain was measured. General strain theory has done better and its predicted conditioning effects have been found, but effects are generally modest, what counts as "strain" differs widely across studies, and reviewers were still calling its empirical status an open question in 2007.

compareContrast.distinction: Merton explains differing rates of deviance across a society's groups from one structural mismatch between cultural goals and legitimate means. Agnew explains one person's offending from any disliked event or condition, through negative emotion, moderated by that person's coping resources, supports, and associates.

Both depart from the approved means, but innovation keeps the society's success goal and simply reaches it another way, while rebellion discards the goal as well and substitutes a new set of goals and standards, seeking to change the structure rather than to win inside it.

Cohen explains why strained youths form an alternative status system - the strain is about standing, not money. Cloward and Ohlin explain why strained youths in different neighbourhoods end up in different kinds of groups, because illegitimate opportunities are themselves unequally available.

Strain theories ask what motivates a normally law-abiding person into crime and answer with pressure. Control theories assume the motivation is already general and ask instead what usually restrains people. Agnew wrote general strain theory partly to restore strain's standing after critiques such as Hirschi's in 1969 and Kornhauser's in 1978 had pushed it to the margins.

keyTakeaway: Strain theory is two theories under one name: Merton's structural claim that a culture can push people toward crime by demanding a goal it does not equip everyone to reach, and Agnew's social-psychological claim that disliked events produce anger and that anger sometimes produces crime, depending on what else a person has to draw on. The second has held up better in testing than the first, and neither explains crime in general.

questionBank.prompt: In Merton's 1938 typology, which mode of adaptation accepts the culturally prescribed goals while eliminating the institutionalized means of reaching them?
options: Ritualism
Innovation
Retreatism
Conformity
questionBank.explanation: Merton's table marks innovation plus on culture goals and minus on institutionalized means. Ritualism is the reverse, minus on goals and plus on means. Retreatism eliminates both. Conformity accepts both and is, Merton wrote, the most common and widely diffused adaptation in every society.
questionBank.skill: Recalling Merton's five modes of adaptation and their sign values

questionBank.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three sources of strain Agnew set out in his 1992 general strain theory?
options: The actual or anticipated failure to achieve positively valued goals
The actual or anticipated removal of positively valued stimuli
The actual or anticipated presentation of negatively valued stimuli
Weak attachment to conventional others such as parents and teachers
questionBank.explanation: Agnew named three types of strain: failure to achieve positively valued goals, removal of positively valued stimuli, and presentation of negatively valued stimuli, each actual or anticipated. Weak attachment to conventional others is a social bond variable from control theory, which Agnew explicitly distinguished general strain theory from.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing general strain theory's sources of strain from control-theory concepts

questionBank.prompt: A seventeen-year-old loses a place on a team central to how she sees herself, is threatened daily by another student, and has no adult she trusts enough to tell. She starts fighting at school. Which reading of this case best matches general strain theory as Agnew stated it?
options: Two strains are present, the removal of something valued and the presentation of something noxious; both are large and readily seen as unjust, they generate anger, and the absence of social support and of practised legal coping makes a criminal response more likely.
She accepted the cultural goal of athletic success but eliminated the institutionalized means, which is the innovation adaptation.
Weak institutions in her neighbourhood failed to supervise her, which is the central claim of general strain theory.
She acquired fighting through imitation of peers and reinforcement for it, which is what general strain theory means by coping.
questionBank.explanation: The case has two of Agnew's three strain types, both high in magnitude and easily perceived as unjust, which is the profile his 2001 criteria mark as criminogenic; the pathway is anger and the conditioning factors are the missing social support and coping resources. Innovation is Merton's category and concerns approved means to a success goal, not this case. Neighbourhood institutions belong to social disorganisation, and imitation and reinforcement belong to social learning theory.
questionBank.skill: Applying general strain theory's strain types, emotional mechanism, and conditioning factors to a case

questionBank.prompt: Why is Merton's strain theory usually described as structural while Agnew's general strain theory is described as largely social-psychological?
options: Merton wrote earlier, and criminology as a discipline simply became more psychological over time.
Merton studied adults while Agnew studied adolescents, and adolescent behaviour is psychological.

Merton explains differing rates of deviance across a society's groups from the arrangement of cultural goals and legitimate means, whereas Agnew explains an individual's offending through disliked events, the emotions they produce, and that person's coping resources and associates.
Merton relied on official crime statistics, which are macro-level data, while Agnew relied on self-report surveys, which are individual-level data.
questionBank.explanation: The difference is the unit of analysis and the mechanism, not chronology, sample age, or data source. Merton's individuals are occupants of structural positions and his closing acknowledged he had not tested the scheme against group variations in deviance rates; Agnew's variables - subjective strain, anger, coping skills, social support, self-efficacy, temperament - are properties of persons, which is why reviewers call his theory a social-psychological interpretation of delinquency.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a theory's level of explanation from its variables and mechanism

questionBank.prompt: What do published reviews report about the empirical testing of classic Mertonian strain theory?
options: Tests have consistently confirmed it, which is why it remains criminology's dominant explanation of offending.
Results have been mixed, with the level of support depending heavily on how strain was operationalized - most often, and by later accounts wrongly, as the gap between aspirations and expectations.
It has never been tested empirically, because its central concepts cannot be measured in survey research.
Tests have uniformly rejected it, and no study using any measure has reported supportive evidence.
questionBank.explanation: Burton and Cullen's 1992 review reported mixed results with support varying by the operationalization of strain. Agnew and colleagues argued in 1996 that the usual aspirations-versus-expectations measure was the wrong one and that directly measuring dissatisfaction with monetary status yielded qualified support, unlike much previous research. So the theory has been tested extensively, has not been uniformly rejected, and is not confirmed or dominant.
questionBank.skill: Evaluating how measurement choices shape a theory's apparent empirical support
